Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 15, verse 1:

Page 8

﴿Alif. Lam. Ra.﴾ The discussion of the like of this opening of this surah has already passed, at the beginning of Surah Yunus.

And it has already passed, at the beginning of Surah al-Baqarah, what these openings contain of a proclamation of the challenge (tahaddi) by the inimitability (i'jaz) of the Qur'an.

﴿These are the verses of the Book and a clear Qur'an.﴾ The demonstrative refers to what is known before this surah of the measure of what has been sent down of the Qur'an; that is: the verses that are known to you and distinguished for you with a distinction like the distinction of a thing to which a pointing gesture can be made, are the verses of the Book. This demonstrative places the verses of the Qur'an in the position of what is present and witnessed.

"Al-Kitab" (the Book) is a proper name by predominance (alam bi-l-ghalabah) for the Qur'an that was sent down to Muhammad (ﷺ) as guidance and direction to the law (shari'ah). It was called a "kitab" because they were commanded to write down what was revealed of it, for its preservation and for reviewing it. Thus the Qur'an was called a Book before it was written down and collected, because it is of the nature of a book.

This verse occurs at the opening of a warning to those who deny the Qur'an, for the purpose of giving them an excuse (i'dhar) by calling them to consider the proofs of the truthfulness of the Messenger (ﷺ) and the truth of his religion.

Since the basic function of the definite article "al-" in a noun that has become a proper name by predominance is to use the article as a means of indicating the sense of the perfection of the species in what is defined, the proper name by predominance did not lose the sense that it is superior within its species by the help of the context. Thus it required that those verses be verses of a Book that reaches the utmost perfection of its species, that is: of the books of the laws.

Page 9

He coordinated "wa-Qur'an" (and a Qur'an) with "al-Kitab", because the name "Qur'an" was made a proper name for what was sent down to Muhammad (ﷺ) for inimitability and legislation. So it is the proper name of the Book of Islam, like the names Torah, Gospel and Psalms for the books known by those names.

The name "Qur'an" is firmer in defining it than "Kitab", because the original proper name (alam asli) enters more deeply into defining the named than the proper name by predominance. So whether the word "Qur'an" is indefinite or defined with "al-", it is a proper name for the Book of Islam. If it is indefinite, its indefiniteness is on the original basis of proper names; if it is defined, its definiteness is to recall the original sense before it became a proper name, like the definiteness of proper names that are transferred from active participles; because the Qur'an is transferred from the verbal noun that signifies recitation, that is: the thing recited which, when it is recited, is the utmost of recitation.

In naming by the verbal noun there is, as is known, a sense of intensifying the attribute of the root of the verbal noun. And in order to indicate what is in each of the two proper names of a meaning not in the other, it is good to combine them by coordination, and this is of what is expressed as coordination of explanation (atf al-tafsir); because "Qur'an" stands in the position of an explanatory apposition (atf al-bayan) to "Kitab", and it resembles coordination of an attribute to the thing described and what is part of it, but it is more like it, because the coordinated term is followed by a descriptive attribute, which is "clear" (mubin). All of this is considered in terms of meaning.

He began with the definite article because in the definite there is an announcement of fame and clarity and what it contains of indicating the sense of perfection. And because the defined is the basis of the predication and the attributes. Then the indefinite was brought, because its attribute "clear" was intended, and the indefinite is more suitable for applying attributes to it; and because indefiniteness indicates magnification and exaltation. So the two indications were distributed between the point of definiteness and the point of indefiniteness.

As for placing "al-Kitab" before "al-Qur'an" in mention: this is because the context of the speech is a rebuke of the disbelievers and a warning to them that a time will come when they will wish that they had been believers. So when the speech was directed at the deniers, it was fitting to bring to mind what was sent down to Muhammad (ﷺ) by its more general title, which is being a Book; because when they disputed, they disputed only about a Book, and they said: ﴿If only a Book had been sent down to us, we would have been better guided than them﴾ [al-An'am: 157]; and because they know what other nations possess by the title "Book", and they know them by the title "People of the Book".

As for the title "Qur'an", it suits the Book being read and studied, and it is only believers in it who read and study it. For this reason the title "Qur'an" was placed first in Surah al-Naml, as will come.

"Mubin" is the active participle of abana, the intransitive form which has the meaning of "bana" (to be clear), used for emphasis on its manifestness, that is: the manifestness of its great Qur'anic quality, that is: the manifestness of its inimitability which the opponents and others have realized.

We did not make "mubin" in the sense of the transitive "abana" (to make clear), because its being clear in itself is more forceful in rebuking its deniers than describing it as showing what it contains. A close parallel to this verse will come at the beginning of Surah al-Naml.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 15, verse 2:

﴿Perhaps those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims.﴾

This is a fresh, independent sentence (isti'naf ibtida'i), and it is the opening of the main theme; what precedes it serves as a warning and admonition.

"Rubama" (perhaps / sometimes) is composed of "rubba," a particle that indicates indefiniteness in what follows it, governs the noun in the genitive, and applies only to nouns. The ba' in it is read both with and without shedding, in all cases, and there are several dialectal forms of it.

Nafi', 'Asim and Abu Ja'far read it with the ba' lightened (rubama), and the rest of the readers read it with the ba' doubled (rubbama).

The particle "rubba" is joined by "ma" (al-kaffah, the "restraining ma"), which stops it from governing. Its attachment after "rubba" generally cancels its governing effect, and by this it becomes possible for it to enter upon verbs. When it enters upon a verb, what is usually meant is diminution (taqlil).

Most often the verb is in the past tense, but it may also be in the present tense to indicate the future, as here, and there is no need to interpret it as past in terms of certainty.

Some grammarians required that it enter only upon the past tense, and they interpreted verses like this one as if the verb were in the past tense because its occurrence is certain. The sense of the future here is clear, because the disbelievers did not wish to be Muslims before the strength of Islam became manifest from the time of the Hijrah.

The statement is a report used in the sense of threat and dread concerning their not following the religion of Islam. The meaning is: those who disbelieved may well wish that they had become Muslims.

The diminution here is used in the sense of mockery and intimidation, i.e., "Beware of your wish that you were Muslims, for it may well happen rarely," as the Arabs say in rebuke, "Perhaps you will regret your action," while they do not doubt his regret; they only mean that if regret were doubtful, it would still be incumbent upon you to do what you may regret neglecting, so that you would not regret it, because the sensible person guards against a suspected harm just as he guards against a certain one.

The meaning is that they may wish they had become Muslims, but after it is too late.

The use of the past form of the verb "to be" indicates that they will wish for Islam after the time of being able to attain it has passed, and that is when they are killed by the hands of the Muslims and when the Day of Recompense arrives. The polytheists have indeed wished for this many times in the worldly life, when they witnessed the victory of the Muslims.

From Ibn Mas'ud: the disbelievers of Quraysh wished this on the Day of Badr when they saw the victory of the Muslims, and they will wish for it in the Hereafter when they are driven to the Fire because of their disbelief. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And on the Day when the wrongdoer will bite on his hands, saying, "Oh, I wish I had taken with the Messenger a way."﴾ [al-Furqan: 27]. Likewise, when the disobedient among the Muslims are brought out of the Fire, those who disbelieved in the Fire will wish they had been Muslims, although they had wished this many times and concealed it within themselves out of obstinacy and disbelief. Allah the Exalted says:

﴿If you could but see when they are made to stand over the Fire and say, "Oh, would that we were returned, and not deny the signs of our Lord, and be among the believers."﴾ [al-An'am: 27] ﴿But there has appeared to them what they used to conceal before.﴾ [al-An'am: 28], meaning: they do not state it openly.

"Law" (if / would that) in ﴿law kanu muslimin﴾ is used to express wishing, because its original function is conditional, being a particle of unfulfilled condition for unfulfilled condition. It is therefore suited to the meaning of wishing, which is the request for a thing whose attainment is impossible. When it comes after something that indicates wishing, it is used in that sense, as if there were an implied verb of saying that the wisher utters, and since the verb of saying was omitted, the reported speech was shifted to indirect report by meaning. Thus the original of ﴿law kanu muslimin﴾ is "law kunna muslimin" (if only we had been Muslims).

The omission of the answer (jawab) of "law" was made obligatory, being sufficed by the context indicating it. Then the omission of the verb of saying became common, so "law" came to convey the sense of the verbal noun (masdariyyah), and the meaning became: those who disbelieved wish for their being Muslims. For this reason, they counted it among the particles of the verbal noun, though the verbal noun is an incidental meaning in the speech and is not what it signifies by convention.

[Page 13]

﴿Leave them to eat and enjoy themselves, and let hope distract them; they will soon know.﴾ Since *rubba* (a particle meaning "how many a," which here indicates paucity) indicates few, it requires that their persistence in their excess is most of their condition, namely turning away from what Islam calls them to of perfection of the soul. By turning away from it, they have accepted for themselves the life of livestock, which is restricting oneself to bodily pleasures. Thus the Messenger (ﷺ) was addressed in a way that alludes to them, that their life is a life of eating and drinking, which is something they are reproached for in the course of their speech, as in the words of al-Hutay'a:

"Leave generosity; do not rise to pursue it. Sit down, for you are the one who eats and is clothed."

They are immersed in what they are reproached for in their deeds. God the Exalted said: ﴿Those who disbelieve enjoy themselves and eat as livestock eat, and the Fire is their abode﴾ [Muhammad: 12].

*Dhar* (ذَرْ, "leave") is an imperative for which no past tense has been heard in their speech, and it means "abandon." It was discussed earlier in His words ﴿And leave those who have taken their religion as amusement and diversion﴾ [al-An'am: 70] in Surat al-An'am.

The command to abandon them is used in its implication, which is the futility of eagerness to reform them. It is not used to grant permission to leave them, because the Prophet (ﷺ) is commanded to persist in calling them. God the Exalted said: ﴿And leave those who have taken their religion as amusement … and remind with it, lest a soul be delivered to destruction for what it has earned﴾ [al-An'am: 70]. He did not command him to leave them except that He followed it with a command to remind with the Qur'an. So it is known that "leaving" is used to mean the absence of hope for their reform. This is like the words of Kabsha, sister of 'Amr ibn Ma'dikarib, concerning the killing of her brother 'Abd Allah, urging her brother 'Amr to take up vengeance for him:

"Leave 'Amr alone; indeed 'Amr is at peace. Is the belly of 'Amr anything but a span for a morsel?"

This verb and what is meant by it may be used as a metonymy (*kinayah*, an indirect expression) for not needing help, or for not accepting intercession, as in His words ﴿Leave Me with the one whom I created alone﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 11], and His words ﴿And leave Me with the deniers﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 11].

It may also be used for figurative abandonment (*majaz*, figurative usage), by placing the addressee in the position of one who is clothed in the opposite, as in the words of Abu Tammam:

"Let me weep before the wailing of the doves, and do not make me a target for the blamers."

Such a statement is said at the point of despair and hopelessness regarding a person's reform.

The object of the verb "leave" has been omitted, because the verb has been placed in the position of what needs no object, since what is meant is abandoning preoccupation with them and keeping away from them. For this reason the verb "leave" was made to take their persons directly, to indicate despair of them.

*Ya'kulu* (يَأْكُلُوا, "they eat") is in the jussive mood by the elided imperative *lam* (لام الأمر, the "lam of command"), as was explained earlier at His words ﴿Say to My servants who have believed: let them establish prayer﴾ [Ibrahim: 31] in Surat Ibrahim. It is

[Page 14]

a command of rebuke, threat, and warning, as indicated by His words "they will soon know." It is like His words ﴿Eat and enjoy yourselves a little; indeed you are criminals﴾ [al-Mursalat: 46].

It is not good to make it jussive as an answer to *dharhum* (ذَرْهم, "leave them"), because they eat and enjoy themselves whether the Messenger (ﷺ) abandons calling them or calls them.

*Tamatti'* (التَّمَتُّع, "enjoyment") means benefiting from provisions. It has been mentioned more than once, among them His words ﴿And provision for a time﴾ [al-A'raf: 24] in Surat al-A'raf.

The distraction of hope to them (*ilha' al-amal*) means causing them to forget what it was their duty to remember, by diverting them, through pursuing what they do not attain, from thinking about resurrection, life, and the Hereafter.

*Amal* (الأمل, "hope") is a verbal noun, and it is the presumption that a desired thing will occur while considering its occurrence unlikely. It is thus intermediate between *raja'* (رجاء, "hope") and *tama'* (طمع, "desire"). Do you not see the words of Ka'b:

"I hope and aspire that her affection will draw near, and I do not think there is any granting from you to us."

The allusion is followed by explicit threat in His words ﴿they will soon know﴾, which is among the expressions frequently used for threat until it became almost literal. In it there is an indication that their respite has a known term, like His words ﴿And they will soon know when they see the punishment﴾ [al-Furqan: 42].

[Page 15]

This is a parenthetical concluding clause (i'tiraḍ tadhyili, a clause inserted to round off the preceding statement), because this sentence contains a ruling that applies to them, namely the ruling on the respite granted to nations against whom destruction has been decreed. That is, We did not destroy any nation without first granting it enjoyment for a period of time, and its destruction had a fixed term and a determined time. It enjoys its provision before that time arrives, and it is seized when that time comes.

This is an allusion (ta'rid) to a threat and a warning, reinforced by comparing them with the earlier deniers. He mentioned the condition of the towns that were destroyed before them only to remind these people of God's way of granting respite to wrongdoers, lest what they are enjoying deceive them into thinking they have escaped the warning. This threat does not imply that God has appointed a term for the destruction of the polytheists, for God did not uproot them entirely, but He guided many of them to Islam by the sword and destroyed their leaders on the day of Badr.

The qaryah (town) here means the city. It was discussed earlier in His words, ﴿Or like the one who passed by a town﴾ (al-Baqarah: 259) in Surat al-Baqarah.

The kitab (decree) means the determined measure with God. It is likened to a book in that it admits of no increase or decrease, and it is known to God: "My Lord neither errs nor forgets."

The clause ﴿and it has a known decree﴾ is in the position of a ḥāl (circumstantial clause). Its being joined by the conjunction wāw is sufficient evidence for this, since it is an exception from a general set of circumstances. The one it describes is qaryah, and although it is a nakirah (indefinite noun), its occurrence in a context of negation (siyaq al-nafy) permitted a ḥāl to come from it, just as generality permits a predicate about an indefinite noun to be valid.

The clause ﴿No nation precedes its term﴾ is a bayan (elaboration) of the clause "﴿and it has a known decree﴾," to explain the benefit of the limitation: that it does not admit of being exceeded, either at its beginning or at its end.

The meaning of (تسبق أجلها, tasbiqu ajalaha, "precedes its term") is that it escapes it, i.e., it is destroyed before its arrival. This is likened to outrunning (sabq). Yastaʾkhirūn means "they delay"; the sīn and tāʾ are for emphasis.

The pronoun referring to al-ummah (the nation) was made feminine singular once, in consideration of the wording, and made masculine plural in consideration of the meaning. The object of yastaʾkhirūn was omitted because it is known, i.e., وما يستأخرون عنه, "nor do they delay from it."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 15, verses 6–7:

[p. 16]
﴿And they say: "O you to whom the Reminder has been sent down, you are truly mad!" "Why do you not bring us the angels, if you are of the truthful?"﴾

This is conjoined to the clause ﴿Leave them to eat and enjoy themselves﴾ (al-Hijr: 3). The connection is that the clause conjoined to it contained their absorption in pleasures and hopes, while this one contains their deep immersion in disbelief and their denial of the Muhammadan message.

The meaning is: leave them to deny and to say all manner of things, of denial and mockery. The whole clause is part of what they say.

The vocative in ﴿O you to whom the Reminder has been sent down﴾ is for publicizing the attribute by which he is addressed. The choice of the relative form (al-mawsuliyya) is for the sense in the relative clause, which they made the cause of their derision. The indicator of the derision is their saying ﴿You are truly mad!﴾ They intended to mock his attribute, so God made them speak the truth about it, diverting their tongues from abuse. This is like the report that "when they reviled the Prophet ﷺ or satirized him, they would call him Mudhammam (the blamed one); so the Prophet ﷺ said to 'A'isha: Do you not see how God has averted from me the harm of the polytheists and their cursing? They curse Mudhammam, but I am Muhammad."

In this, the relative clause is ascribed to the one referred to by the relative pronoun according to what the bearer of the name claims, not according to the speaker's belief, by way of derision.

Al-dhikr: it is the verbal noun of dhakara when it means to utter, and the verbal noun of dhakara when a thing comes to mind. Thus al-dhikr is the revealed speech, meant to be recited and repeated; it is for recitation, because it is mentioned and repeated. Either because in it is the reminder of God and the Last Day, or in the sense that through it there is their mention among others. The verse of the Most High covers both: ﴿We have sent down to you a Book in which is your reminder﴾ (al-Anbiya': 10), and He said ﴿And indeed it is a reminder for you and your people﴾ (al-Zukhruf: 44). The intended meaning here is the Qur'an.

[p. 17]
Naming the Qur'an "dhikr" is a comprehensive and remarkable designation, of which the Arabs had no knowledge before it appeared in the Qur'an.

Likewise its naming as "Qur'an," because the purpose of its descent was that it be recited. Thus dhikr and Qur'an became two categories of speech which are delivered to people for the purpose of understanding and recitation, just as among the kinds of speech were poetry, sermon, narrative and legend.

What confirms this is the Most High's saying ﴿We did not teach him poetry, nor is it fitting for him. It is only a reminder and a clear Qur'an﴾ (Ya Sin: 69). He negated that the Book sent down upon Muhammad ﷺ is poetry, and described it as a reminder and a Qur'an. It is not hidden that describing it thus implies a difference between the described and the description, and this difference is in terms of the meaning in the two attributes which we have pointed to. So the meaning is: it is of the category of dhikr and of the category of Qur'an, not of the category of poetry, nor of the category of legends.

Then, with the definite article, "al-Qur'an" became a proper name by predominance for the Book sent down upon Muhammad ﷺ, as you have known just above.

They described him as mad only because they imagined that claiming the revelation descended upon him could not come from a sane person, since that, in their view, contradicts reality, supposing that what their intellects, which have a veil over them, cannot accept is not something that sane people should accept; so the one who claims it is not sane.

Al-majnun: one who has been driven mad (junna), i.e., afflicted with corruption of the intellect from the effect of jinn touching him, in their belief. Thus al-majnun is a passive participle derived from the verb in the passive voice, and it is among the verbs which occur only with a passive subject.

The emphasis of the clause with (inna) and the lam is because they intended to establish this for him, perhaps he would desist from persisting in it, or because they intended to establish it for the listeners present in their assemblies.

[p. 18]
The clause ﴿Why do you not bring us the angels﴾ is an argument for what the preceding clause implied, in that its purpose is to deny the Messenger ﷺ, because what comes from a madman in speech does not conform to reality, so most of it is false.

"Lawma" is a particle of restriction, equivalent to the exhortative "lawla," and it is required that it be followed by a verbal clause.

The meaning of bringing the angels is their presence with them, so that they may inform them of his truthfulness in the message. This is like what God related in another verse, in the saying of the Most High: ﴿Or you bring God and the angels as a guarantee﴾ (al-Isra': 92).

And ﴿of the truthful﴾ means: of the people whose attribute is truthfulness. This is stronger than "if you are truthful," as was mentioned earlier in the saying of the Most High ﴿Be with the truthful﴾ (al-Tawba: 119) in Surat Bara'a, and in His saying ﴿He said: I seek refuge in God from being among the ignorant﴾ (al-Baqara: 67) in Surat al-Baqara.

The meaning of bringing the angels is their presence with them, so that they may inform them of his truthfulness in the message. This is like what God related in another verse, in the saying of the Most High: ﴿Or you bring God and the angels as a guarantee﴾ (al-Isra': 92).

And ﴿of the truthful﴾ means: of the people whose attribute is truthfulness. This is stronger than "if you are truthful," as was mentioned earlier in the saying of the Most High ﴿Be with the truthful﴾ (al-Tawba: 119) in Surat Bara'a, and in His saying ﴿He said: I seek refuge in God from being among the ignorant﴾ (al-Baqara: 67) in Surat al-Baqara.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 15, verse 8:

﴿We do not send down the angels except with truth, and they would not then be given respite.﴾

It is a resumed initial sentence (mustaʼnafa ibtidaʼiyya), an answer to their speech, their doubts (shubuhat) and their demands (muqtarahat).

The answer begins by removing their doubt, when they said ﴿Why do you not bring us the angels?﴾ [al-Hijr: 7]. What is intended by it is the removal of their ignorance, since they asked for the descent of the angels as a sign of confirmation. Even though they sought this with the intent of mockery (tahakkum), they nonetheless believed that the descent of the angels is the sign of the truthfulness of the Messenger ﷺ. Their answer therefore came mixed with an element of the wise method (al-uslub al-hakim), which is to turn them toward being taught the distinction (al-mayz) between the signs of the Messengers and the signs of punishment. God willed not to withhold guidance from them, although they were deserving of not being answered.

Al-nuzul (descent) is descending from a height to a lower place. What is meant by it here is the passage of the angels from the upper world to the earthly world, a specific descent: their descent to execute God's command with a punishment He sends upon the disbelievers, just as they were sent down to the cities of Lut (peace be upon him). It is not like the descent of Jibril (peace be upon him) or of other angels to the Messengers (peace be upon them) with the laws or with revelation. God, the Exalted, said regarding Zakariyya (peace be upon him): ﴿So the angels called him while he was standing in prayer in the sanctuary: "Indeed, God gives you good tidings of Yahya"﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 39].

What is meant by "al-haqq" (the truth) here is the thing that is inevitably come, i.e., the decreed thing, like the use of "qada'" (decree) to mean "maqdi" (what is decreed). Here it is an attribute of an omitted noun understood from the context, i.e., the inevitable punishment (al-'adhab al-haqq). God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And upon many the punishment has become due﴾ [al-Hajj: 18]. This is supported by His saying ﴿and they would not then be given respite﴾, meaning: the angels do not descend to people other than the Messengers and Prophets (peace and blessings be upon them) except accompanying the inevitable punishment upon the people, as the angels descended upon the people of Lut, which was the punishment of annihilation (isti'sal). Had the angels descended, the ones upon whom they were sent down would have been hastened (to destruction) and would not have been reprieved.

From this it is understood that God grants them respite, because He did not intend their annihilation; He intended that the spread of the religion should be through them, so He reprieved them until they were guided, but He destroyed their chiefs and their planners.

A parallel to this is the saying of God, the Exalted, in Surat al-An'am: ﴿And they said, "Why was an angel not sent down to him?" Had We sent down an angel, the matter would have been decided, and then they would not be respited﴾ [al-An'am: 8]. The angels did descend upon them on the day of Badr, cutting off the heads of the polytheists.

Al-in-zar (respite) is delay and postponement.

And "idha" (then) is a particle of answer and consequence. It has been dropped here between the two parts of its answer, out of regard for the coordination of its answer with His saying ﴿We do not send down the angels﴾. The usual position of "idhan" (then) is at the beginning of its answer. Its clause is the intended answer to their saying ﴿Why do you not bring us the angels?﴾ [al-Hijr: 7], while the clause ﴿We do not send down the angels except with truth﴾ is placed before it by inversion, because it is a justification for the answer. It was placed first because it is more effective in the rebuttal, and because it is more conducive to the brevity of the answer.

The sense of the speech is: "Why do you not bring us the angels, if you are of the truthful? Then you would not have been respited in life, and destruction would have been hastened upon you; for the angels do not descend except accompanied by the inevitable punishment." This meaning occurs in His saying: ﴿And they ask you to hasten the punishment. Had there not been a specified term, the punishment would have come upon them﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 53].

The majority (al-Jumhur) read "ma tanazzalu" with a fatha on the ta', on the basis that its origin is "tatanazzalu."

Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, read it with a damma on the ta' and a fatha on the za', in the passive voice, with "al-malaika" in the nominative as deputy of the subject.

Al-Kisa'i, Hafs from 'Asim, and Khalaf read ﴿ma nunazzilu al-malaikata﴾ with a nun at its beginning, a kasra on the za', and "al-malaika" in the accusative as the object.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 15, verse 9:**

﴿Indeed, it is We who sent down the Reminder, and indeed, We will be its guardian.﴾

This is a resumptive sentence (*istinaf ibtida'i*, a sentence that begins a new topic) that refutes part of what the mockers said to him when they said, ﴿O you to whom the Reminder has been revealed, you are surely mad!﴾ [al-Hijr: 6], after he had already quickly addressed their doubt in their saying, ﴿Why do you not bring us the angels, if you are of the truthful?﴾ [al-Hijr: 7].

The two answers are presented in the reverse order of the two statements (*nashr* in reverse of *laff*), with attention to beginning with the response to their second statement, because of the doubt it contains, through the challenge to produce something and the silencing of the opponent. Then the discourse turns to refuting their allusive mockery and their demand to see the angels.

This answer is a form of *qawl bi-l-muwjab* (accepting the premise of the opponent's claim), by affirming the sending down of the Reminder upon the Messenger ﷺ, following the apparent meaning of their words.

The aim is to refute them in their mockery, so the statement is emphasized with *inna* ("indeed") and with the separating pronoun (*damir al-fasl*), which also agrees with what is the case in reality, as in His saying, ﴿They say, "We testify that you are surely the Messenger of God." God knows that you are indeed His Messenger, and God testifies that the hypocrites are surely liars.﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 1].

**[p. 21]**

Then this is raised to a higher level and to a stronger rebuke for them, by saying that the One who sent down the Reminder is also its guardian from the plots of enemies. So the clause ﴿and indeed, We will be its guardian﴾ is a parenthetical clause (*mu'taridah*), and the *waw* is parenthetical (*i'tiradiyyah*).

The pronoun governed by the *lam* refers to the Reminder, and the *lam* strengthens the operation of the governing word because it is weakened by being placed after its object.

Its guarding includes protection from perishing, and protection from addition and loss in it, by making its transmission (*tawatur*) and the means to that easy, and by preserving it from alteration and change, until the Ummah memorized it in the hearts from the lifetime of the Prophet ﷺ. It thus settled among the Ummah by being heard from the Prophet ﷺ, and its memorizers reached the number required for *tawatur* in every region.

Iyad related in *al-Madarik* that the judge Isma'il ibn Ishaq ibn Hammad al-Maliki al-Basri was asked about the secret behind the occurrence of change in the earlier books and the preservation of the Qur'an from means of alteration. He answered that God entrusted the rabbis with the preservation of their books, so He said, ﴿for they were required to guard the Book of God﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 44], and He Himself took charge of guarding the Qur'an, so He said, ﴿Indeed, it is We who sent down the Reminder, and indeed, We will be its guardian.﴾ Abu al-Hasan ibn al-Muntab said: I mentioned this statement to al-Muhamili, and he said to me, "There is nothing better than this statement."

**[p. 22]**

In the *Tafsir* of al-Qurtubi, in a report he narrated from Yahya ibn Aktham, he mentioned the story of the conversion to Islam of a Jewish man in the time of al-Ma'mun. He related it to Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna, and Sufyan said: God said in the Torah and the Gospel, ﴿for they were required to guard the Book of God﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 44], so He made its preservation their responsibility, and it was lost. And He, Mighty and Majestic, said, ﴿Indeed, it is We who sent down the Reminder, and indeed, We will be its guardian,﴾ so God preserved it for us and it was not lost. End of quotation. Perhaps this is a coincidence of thoughts (*tawarud al-khawatir*).

With this, along with the honoring of the status of the Qur'an, there is a provocation to the polytheists, in that the matter of this religion will be completed, the Qur'an will spread, and it will remain across the passing ages. This is a form of challenge, so that this statement serves as evidence that the Qur'an was sent down from God, as a sign of the truthfulness of the Messenger ﷺ. For if it were the speech of humans, or if it were not a sign, it would be subject to addition and loss, and it would contain contradiction. God, the Exalted, said, ﴿Do they not then reflect on the Qur'an? Had it been from other than God, they would have found in it much contradiction.﴾ [al-Nisa': 82].

The passage is conjoined (ʿuṭifa) to the statement ﴿Indeed, it is We who sent down the Reminder, and indeed We will be its guardian﴾ [15:9], on the basis that the earlier statement is a response to their mockery in their words ﴿O you to whom the Reminder has been sent down, indeed you are mad﴾ [15:6]. The statement ﴿Indeed, it is We who sent down the Reminder﴾ [15:9] is a statement in accordance with their own claim (qawl bi-mūjab, a statement that follows from what the opponent has said) ﴿O you to whom the Reminder has been sent down﴾ [15:6]. The statement ﴿Indeed We sent [messengers] before you among the sects of the former peoples﴾ is a refutation of their mockery by way of comparison (tamthīl) with their counterparts among the earlier nations.

In this comparison there is a confirmation of their disbelief, because the disbelief of those earlier peoples is established among the nations and is spoken of among them.

It also contains an implicit warning (taʿrīḍ) to those like them, and an incidental inclusion (idmāj) by way of allusion (kināya) that consoles the Messenger (ﷺ).

Page 23

The emphasis through the oath particle (lām al-qasam) and (qad) is to establish that the sending of messengers by God preceded, like the sending that they denied and found strange, as in His saying ﴿Is it a wonder for the people that We revealed to a man from among them…﴾ [10:2]. This is what the position of the phrase "before you" (min qablika) requires.

Al-shiyaʿ (sects) is the plural of shīʿa, which is a group whose affair is one. This was discussed at His saying ﴿or confuse you into sects﴾ [6:65] in Sūrat al-Anʿām, and it comes at His saying ﴿Then We will surely drag out from every sect﴾ [19:69] in Sūrat Maryam. The meaning is: among the nations of the former peoples, that is, the earlier generations. Some of the nations were sent messengers, and some of them were not sent messengers. This is the reason for the idāfa (genitive construction) of shiyaʿ to al-awwalīn (the former).

﴿And they used to mock him﴾ indicates that this recurred from them and that it was their practice. Thus (kāna, "they used to be") indicates that it was an innate disposition of theirs, and the present tense (muḍāriʿ) indicates its recurrence among them.

The object of "We sent" is elided, indicated by the form of the verb: that is, messengers (rusulan). It is indicated also by His saying "a messenger" (min rasūl).

The fronting of the prepositional phrase before "they mock" (yastahziʾūn) conveys restriction (qaṣr) for the sake of emphasis (mubālagha). This is because, since they used to frequently mock their messenger and this had become their disposition, they were placed in the position of one who has no activity except mocking the Messenger.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 15, verse 12–13:

﴿Thus do We thread it into the hearts of the guilty.﴾ ﴿They do not believe in it, though the way of the former peoples has already passed.﴾ This is a resumptive explanatory statement (isti'naf bayani) arising from a question that occurs to the listener upon His saying: ﴿And there comes not to them a messenger but they mock him﴾ [al-Hijr: 11]. The listener asks: how is it that these nations converged upon one path of misguidance, and the call of the messengers, peace be upon them, did not benefit them? As Almighty God said: ﴿Did they charge one another with it? Nay, they are a rebellious people.﴾

Page 24
The sentence is also a resumptive explanatory statement arising from the sentence ﴿And indeed We are its guardians﴾ [al-Hijr: 9], for it may occur to the mind that the preservation of the Reminder requires that no one who disbelieves in it should disbelieve. The answer is that this is a punishment from God upon them for their criminality and for their receiving the truth with mockery and lack of reflection. For this reason the description "the guilty" (al-mujrimin) was chosen for them rather than "the disbelievers" (al-kafirin), because the attribute of disbelief had become for them like a title that does not convey the meaning of causation. A parallel to this is His saying in another verse: ﴿As for those in whose hearts is a disease, it adds to them uncleanness upon their uncleanness﴾ [al-Tawbah: 125].

The use of the present tense in "naslukuhu" (We thread it) indicates that the intended threading is in the time of the present, i.e., the time of the revelation of the Qur'an, so that it is known that the intention is to explain the reception of the Qur'an by the polytheists. Thus it is not supposed that what is meant by "the guilty" is the followers of the earlier peoples, along with what the present tense conveys of renewal, which is appropriate to His saying: ﴿and the way of the former peoples has already passed﴾, i.e., the conveying of the Qur'an to these people has been renewed according to the custom of conveying messages to those before them. In it there is an allusion that this is a warning to them so that the punishment may descend upon them as it descended upon those before them.

The one referred to by His saying "thus" (kadhalika) is the threading derived from "naslukuhu," in the manner of its like established in His saying: ﴿And thus We have made you a middle nation﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143] in Surat al-Baqarah.

Al-salk (threading) means insertion. Al-A'sha said:

"As the thread enters the bead-hole..." (kama salaka al-sakki fi al-bab fayataqu)

That is: like the threading which we will describe, We thread the Reminder into the hearts of the guilty, i.e., thus We insert the Qur'an into the minds of the polytheists; they hear it and understand it, since it is in their own speech, and they perceive its distinctive features, but it does not settle in their minds with the settledness of belief in it. Rather they are deniers of it, as He said: ﴿And when a surah is sent down, some of them say: "Which of you has had its faith increased by this?" As for those who believe, it has increased them in faith, and they rejoice﴾ [al-Tawbah: 124], ﴿As for those in whose hearts is a disease, it adds to them uncleanness upon their uncleanness, and they die while they are disbelievers﴾ [al-Tawbah: 125].

Page 25
By this threading the proof is established against them, through the conveying of the Qur'an to them, and their hearing of it is repeated time after time, so that the proof may be established.

The pronoun in "naslukuhu" and "bihi" refers to the Reminder in His saying: ﴿Indeed, We sent down the Reminder﴾ [al-Hijr: 9], i.e., the Qur'an.

The guilty are the disbelievers of Quraysh.

The clause "they do not believe in it" is either an explanation of the threading that is compared, or a circumstantial clause (hal) from "the guilty," i.e., their minds comprehend it but they do not believe in it. This is general, and what is meant is those among them who died in disbelief; and the meaning is that they do not believe at any time.

The clause ﴿and the way of the former peoples has already passed﴾ is parenthetical between the clause "they do not believe in it" and the clause "And if We opened for them a gate from the heaven..."

The statement is an allusion to a threat that what befell the earlier nations will befall them, treating the like with its like; for the fact that the custom of the former peoples has passed is a known matter, and mentioning it is not beneficial, so the report is used for its implication, by way of the evidence that taking the statement literally as a mere report is impossible.

Al-sunnah: the familiar custom. It was mentioned in His saying: ﴿Indeed, there have passed before you precedents (sunan)﴾ [Al 'Imran: 137] in Surat Al 'Imran. Its attribution to "the former ones" is by way of its connection to them; in truth it is the sunnah of God concerning them, since that is what is intended here, and the attribution is due to the slightest connection.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 15, verses 14–15:

﴿And if We opened for them a gate from the sky, and they continued to ascend through it,﴾ ﴿they would surely say: "Our eyes have only been dazzled; rather, we are a people bewitched."﴾

This is connected (ʿuṭifa) to the clause "﴿they do not believe in it﴾" [al-Hijr: 13], and it is a comprehensive statement refuting all their excuses, from their saying "﴿Why do you not bring us the angels?﴾" [al-Hijr: 7] and their saying "﴿Indeed, you are a madman﴾" [al-Hijr: 6].

Because they do not seek the proof of his truthfulness, since the signs of truth are clear, but they adopt various excuses.

The comprehensive statement that refutes their excuses is this: if God had opened a gate from the sky when they asked for a sign confirming the truth of the Messenger (ﷺ), i.e., at a request from the Messenger, so that they connected with the world of holiness and the angelic souls and saw that with their own eyes, they would have made excuses, saying that these were imaginations and that they had been bewitched, so they would see what is not a thing as a thing.

A similar verse is His saying: ﴿And if We had sent down to you a book on paper, and they had touched it with their hands, those who disbelieved would have said, "This is nothing but obvious magic."﴾ [al-An'am: 7].

(Ẓalla) indicates continuance during the day, i.e., that this occurred in the full light of day, with the figures clearly visible and no doubt about what is seen.

Al-ʿurūj: the ascent. Its present-tense form (yaʿrujūn) may be read with a ḍamma on the rāʾ, which is the reading attested, or with a kasra; i.e., they would be ascending through that gate during the day.

Suggarat is read with a ḍamma on the sīn and a shadda on the kāf in the recitation of the majority (al-Jumhur), and with a light kāf (takhfīf) in the recitation of Ibn Kathir. In both readings it is in the passive voice, meaning "were shut/blocked," from sakkara al-bāb (with shadda) or sakara (without shadda), meaning to close the door.

The meaning: they would have denied that they had seen anything at all.

The expression is in the form of restriction (ḥaṣr), to indicate that they have firmly settled their statement on this matter. Some of them rebut others, suspecting that they may have seen the gates of heaven and ascended through them, and they claim that they were not seeing. Then they shift from this to the wavering, bewildered stance, moving from one supposition to another, and they say: "Rather, we are a people bewitched," i.e., what we saw is the imaginings of one who is bewitched. Thus they return to placing the blame for this on the Messenger (ﷺ), claiming that he bewitched them when he asked God to open for them a gate from the sky, and He opened it for them.

The discussion of magic and its conditions was already given when He, exalted is He, said: ﴿They teach people magic﴾ [al-Baqarah: 102] in Surat al-Baqarah.

﴿And if We opened for them a gate from the sky, and they continued to ascend through it,﴾ ﴿they would surely say: "Our eyes have only been dazzled; rather, we are a people bewitched."﴾

This is connected (ʿuṭifa) to the clause "﴿they do not believe in it﴾" [al-Hijr: 13], and it is a comprehensive statement refuting all their excuses, from their saying "﴿Why do you not bring us the angels?﴾" [al-Hijr: 7] and their saying "﴿Indeed, you are a madman﴾" [al-Hijr: 6].

Because they do not seek the proof of his truthfulness, since the signs of truth are clear, but they adopt various excuses.

The comprehensive statement that refutes their excuses is this: if God had opened a gate from the sky when they asked for a sign confirming the truth of the Messenger (ﷺ), i.e., at a request from the Messenger, so that they connected with the world of holiness and the angelic souls and saw that with their own eyes, they would have made excuses, saying that these were imaginations and that they had been bewitched, so they would see what is not a thing as a thing.

A similar verse is His saying: ﴿And if We had sent down to you a book on paper, and they had touched it with their hands, those who disbelieved would have said, "This is nothing but obvious magic."﴾ [al-An'am: 7].

(Ẓalla) indicates continuance during the day, i.e., that this occurred in the full light of day, with the figures clearly visible and no doubt about what is seen.

Al-ʿurūj: the ascent. Its present-tense form (yaʿrujūn) may be read with a ḍamma on the rāʾ, which is the reading attested, or with a kasra; i.e., they would be ascending through that gate during the day.

Suggarat is read with a ḍamma on the sīn and a shadda on the kāf in the recitation of the majority (al-Jumhur), and with a light kāf (takhfīf) in the recitation of Ibn Kathir. In both readings it is in the passive voice, meaning "were shut/blocked," from sakkara al-bāb (with shadda) or sakara (without shadda), meaning to close the door.

The meaning: they would have denied that they had seen anything at all.

The expression is in the form of restriction (ḥaṣr), to indicate that they have firmly settled their statement on this matter. Some of them rebut others, suspecting that they may have seen the gates of heaven and ascended through them, and they claim that they were not seeing. Then they shift from this to the wavering, bewildered stance, moving from one supposition to another, and they say: "Rather, we are a people bewitched," i.e., what we saw is the imaginings of one who is bewitched. Thus they return to placing the blame for this on the Messenger (ﷺ), claiming that he bewitched them when he asked God to open for them a gate from the sky, and He opened it for them.

When the preceding discourse concerning the disbelief of the polytheists in the message of Muhammad (ﷺ), and what they did in that regard, had run its course, and the foundational principles upon which they built the edifice of their denial were two, namely his refutation of the divinity of their idols and his affirmation of the Resurrection, the Qur'an set out to show them the proofs that God Most High alone is divine. It mentioned the clear proofs from the creation of the heavens and the earth. It then followed them with proofs of the possibility of resurrection from the creation of life and death and the extinction of nations. It followed these with other proofs in His words, Most High, ﴿And indeed, it is We who give life and cause death, and We are the inheritors﴾ [al-Hijr 15:23], and so on. This coincided with the mention of the opening of the gates of heaven in depicting their arrogance in their obstinacy, so the transition to it was a masterful digression (takhallus).

Within this there is a form of argument against their obstinacy, for if they had sought the truth, the evidence in what is from them would have sufficed them, without seeking supernatural marvels.

The report (khabar) is used for reminder and argument, because the meaning of these reports is known to them.

[p. 29]

The discourse opens with the lam of oath and the particle of emphasis (harf al-tahqiq), treating the addressees, who are heedless of drawing this inference, as if they were in doubt. So the discourse is reinforced for them with two emphasizers. The purpose of the emphasis returns to confirming the argument and compelling them to acknowledge it.

Al-burūj (the constellations, sing. burj, with a dammah on the b) literally means a large building built for dwelling or for fortification, and it is synonymous with a palace. God Most High said: ﴿Even if you were in towers built up high﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:78], in Surat al-Nisa'.

That group forms a single shape resembling dots which, if lines were drawn between them, would produce something like the image of an animal or an instrument. They named those stars after the likeness of that shape, and they lie along the path of the sun's course.

The Arabs called them burūj and dārāt by way of a metaphor that became the cause of the naming. They imagined that they were the stations of the sun, because they fixed the time by its direction, that is, the position of the sun in the vault of the sky by day, as it appears to the observer that the sun travels in something like an arc of a circle. They made them twelve stations, corresponding to the number of the months of the solar year. In reality, they are nothing but the directions of regions, each of which faces the earth from a side beyond the sun for a specific period. Then, when the earth's position changes in its orbit each month of the year, the region facing it changes. By the order that exists in them, it became possible to make them signs marking the times when the four seasons and the twelve months arrive. So they fixed for these signs imaginary boundaries, whose places they determined at night by reference to the position of the sun in the day. They repeated the observation day after day. Whenever a month of the year had passed, they fixed for the following month signs in the region facing the sun's position in that period, and so on, until after twelve months they saw that they had returned to the region facing the point from which they had started. So they made that a complete year. The path that the sun is imagined to have traversed during the year they called the circle of the burūj or the zodiac belt. To distinguish these groups of stars from one another, they gave them names of the things to which they likened them, and they added the word burj to them.

The order of these is, starting from the constellation of the entry of the spring season: al-Hamal (Aries), al-Thawr (Taurus), al-Jawza' (Gemini), derived from al-jawz, with a fatha and a sukun on the middle letter, because it lies across the middle of the sky; al-Saratan (Cancer), al-Asad (Leo), al-Sunbula (Virgo), al-Mizan (Libra), al-'Aqrab (Scorpio), al-Qaws (Sagittarius), al-Jady (Capricorn), al-Dalw (Aquarius), al-Hut (Pisces).

For the constellation of Aries they took the month of April, and so on. This happened by coincidence, in that the sun at that time was in the direction of a star-shaped figure that they likened to the dotted outline of the image of a ram. Then it advanced in the argument by noting that these great constellations were made in shapes that are pleasing to the eye, so they were an adornment for those who look, who enjoy beholding them at night. Thus their benefits are numerous.

As for His words, ﴿and We guarded them from every accursed devil﴾, this is an insertion of instruction within the course of the argument. In it there is an affirmation of the infallibility (ismah) of revelation from being subject to addition or subtraction,

[p. 30]

namely that the realms from which revelation descends and in which it travels are preserved from the corrupt elements. It is linked to His words, ﴿and indeed We are its guardians﴾ [al-Hijr 15:9].

For this reason al-Walid ibn al-Mughira said, when he debated with them about the excuses they had prepared for the delegations of the Arabs during the pilgrimage season, should they ask them about this man who claimed prophethood, and they had proposed to say: "He is a soothsayer." By the guarding from the devils is meant guarding them from settling and establishing themselves in the heavens. The word shaytan was discussed earlier in Surat al-Baqarah.

The stoning mentioned in His words, ﴿then a clear flame pursued him﴾, is not the sense intended here, because the exception prevents that in His words: ﴿except one who snatches a hearing, and a clear flame pursues him﴾.

[p. 31]

Stealing the hearing (istiraq al-sam') means stealing it. The form of ifti'al was used to indicate effort and exertion. Its meaning is listening surreptitiously from the speaker, as if the listener steals from the speaker the words he is concealing from him.

Atba'ahu means "followed him." The hamza is extra, like the hamza in abana, meaning "bana" (to be distinct). It was discussed earlier in His words: ﴿So Satan pursued him, and he became one of the misguided﴾ [al-A'raf 7:175], in Surat al-A'raf.

Al-mubin means the manifest, the clear.

In this there is instruction for them that the meteors (shuhub) which they observe falling in the sky are missiles (rujum) against the eavesdropping devils, driving them away from stealing the hearing entirely. They knew this from the days of ignorance (jahiliyyah), but they did not know its cause.

The purpose of preventing the devils from this is preventing them from gaining knowledge of what God willed they should not know of the affairs of creation and the like, which, if the devils cast it into the knowledge of their allies, would be corruption on earth. Perhaps God allowed the devils and their allies some leeway, so He did not prevent the devils from stealing a little that they conveyed to the soothsayers. When God willed the infallibility of revelation, He prevented them from this entirely. He gave the meteors the power to pierce the waves through which the devils who steal the hearing receive, and to tear apart those gradations described in the authentic hadith.

Furthermore, the apparent meaning of the verse does not require more than the eavesdropper's clinging to the heavens in order to obtain revelations, the eavesdropper being keen to obtain them. In the verse of al-Shu'ara' there is something indicating that this eavesdropper casts what he has heard of such revelations to others, in His words: ﴿They cast the hearing, and most of them are liars﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:223].

The creation of meteors for stoning implies that this eavesdropping has been prevented from the devils.

In Surat al-Jinn there is an indication that this was prevented after the mission (ba'thah) and the descent of the Qur'an, in order to secure revelation from being confused with soothsaying among people. Thus what the hadith of 'A'ishah and Abu

[p. 32]

Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with them both) indicates, namely that the jinn stole the hearing, describes the soothsaying of the earlier period, and His words, "they are nothing" . . . describe the final state of their affair.

It has been established by the Book and the Sunnah that there exist created beings called jinn and devils, together with His words: ﴿and the devils, every builder and diver﴾ [Sad 38:37], and so on. Most often the name jinn is restricted to a kind that does not mingle with the thoughts of humans, while the name devils is restricted to a kind whose habit is whispering into the minds of humans by casting corrupt thoughts.

The apparent sense of the authentic reports from the Book and the Sunnah indicates that these created beings are of several kinds, that they float in the atmospheres, in layers beyond the air, and that they connect with the earth. Among them are kinds that have a connection with human souls without bodies, namely whispering (waswasah), and humans are never free of it.

Some apparent reports from the Sunnah indicate that a kind of them has a connection with souls having a special readiness to acquire knowledge of events before they occur, or of events whose occurrence is remote in the customary course of things, so that some souls precede others in knowing them before they normally arrive. These souls are the souls of soothsayers and charlatans. This kind of created being, whether jinn or devils, is the one called the eavesdropper, and it is the one excepted by His words, "except one who snatches a hearing." When this kind connects with those souls that are prepared to mix with it, some of their rational faculties are blocked from others. The blocked faculty gains increased influence in its functions, by what returns to it from the emptying of the intellectual power from busying itself with competition, and turning to it alone. This gives it an ability to exceed the usual limit for its like, so it pierces the boundaries customary for its like to some degree. Sometimes waves reach it that are intermediate between the waves of the air sphere and the waves of the higher layers adjacent to it, beyond the air sphere.

Let us suppose that this layer is what is called the lowest heaven, and that these waves are the waves of the ether (athir), for they preserve sounds, for example.

[p. 33]

Then these waves that reach the minds of people with such dispositions reach them in fragmented, undetailed form. The owners of those souls then use their natural cleverness and shrewdness to assemble and interpret them. They report the outcome of what they have extracted, drawn from among what they have picked up, what they have composed, and what they have interpreted. In hitting upon some truth they vary according to their sharpness of intelligence, clarity of understanding, and ability to compare things, and according to their practice and firmness in handling their profession and the length of time they have spent at it. These are the *kuhhan* (soothsayers). They were numerous among the tribes of the Arabs, and their reputation among their peoples varied according to how often they matched what was in the minds of their peoples. There is no doubt that the simplicity of the minds of a people has some effect. Their peoples considered the long-lived among them closer to being correct in what they foretold. Through their great shrewdness, and their deceiving of their followers, they produce only ambiguous, equivocal speech that admits of several interpretations, so that they cannot be charged with outright falsehood. They leave the interpretation of their words to whatever happens to people in the same kinds of situations to which those words apply. Their speech is free of guidance and of beneficial truths.

By their cunning and their awareness of the fields of the souls and their influences, they committed themselves to casting what they report in a special form, in which short clauses are required to end in rhymed endings (*saj'*). This is because people reckon that the pairing of one clause with its counterpart is a sign that it hits the truth and reality, and that it is a mark of truthfulness. They mostly kept to seclusion and frequently gazed at the stars at night so that their minds would be free. This is the state of the soothsayers, and it rests on deception, trickery and sorcery, together with the use of a special predisposition in the soul and a power that breaks through the familiar barriers.

This is explained by what is in the Book of Adab of Sahih al-Bukhari, from 'Ā'isha: "People asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the soothsayers, and he said, 'They are nothing' (i.e., there is no existence to what they claim). It was said, 'O Messenger of Allah, they sometimes tell us something that turns out to be true.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, 'That word is from the truth which a jinn snatches and then drops into the ear of his friend like the cackling of a hen, and then they mix into it more than a hundred lies.'"

[Page 34]

And what is in the commentary on Surat al-Hijr in Sahih al-Bukhari, from the hadith of Sufyan, from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When Allah decrees a matter in the heaven (i.e., He commands or reveals), the angels strike their wings in submission to His word (for they are commanded, each in his own duty), like a chain on a smooth rock, which penetrates them (i.e., knowledge reaches them, and an approximate analogy is the movements of the apparatus that receives telegraph messages, the telegraph). The eavesdroppers hear it, and the eavesdroppers are one above another (i.e., they are layers differing in height). Sufyan described it with his hand: he tilted it and spread the fingers of his right hand, placing some above others. The eavesdropper hears the word and throws it to the one beneath him, then that one throws it to the one beneath him, until it is cast onto the tongue of the soothsayer or the sorcerer. Sometimes the shooting star overtakes the listener before he casts it, and sometimes he casts it before it overtakes him, and he lies with it a hundred lies. Then they say, 'Did he not tell us that on such-and-such a day such-and-such would happen? And we found it true, because of the word that was heard from the heaven.'"

As for the reports and stories of the soothsayers, most of them are fabrications and lies. The most authentic of them is the hadith of Sawad ibn Qarib in the account of the conversion of 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him), from Sahih al-Bukhari.

All these phenomena require only the perception of what is heard of the speech of the angels. Without doubt they are brought close to what is heard, because they indicate the resolves of angelic souls and their directions toward the things they are employed for.

He expressed it by "hearing" because it ultimately returns to news. What the eavesdropper obtains is the awareness of what the angels are directed to accomplish, and what the soothsayer obtains is likewise. The outcome is that the soothsayer reports it, and so it returns to something heard.

[p. 33]

Then these waves that reach the minds of people with such dispositions reach them in fragmented, undetailed form. The owners of those souls then use their natural cleverness and shrewdness to assemble and interpret them. They report the outcome of what they have extracted, drawn from among what they have picked up, what they have composed, and what they have interpreted. In hitting upon some truth they vary according to their sharpness of intelligence, clarity of understanding, and ability to compare things, and according to their practice and firmness in handling their profession and the length of time they have spent at it. These are the *kuhhan* (soothsayers). They were numerous among the tribes of the Arabs, and their reputation among their peoples varied according to how often they matched what was in the minds of their peoples. There is no doubt that the simplicity of the minds of a people has some effect. Their peoples considered the long-lived among them closer to being correct in what they foretold. Through their great shrewdness, and their deceiving of their followers, they produce only ambiguous, equivocal speech that admits of several interpretations, so that they cannot be charged with outright falsehood. This is because people reckon that the pairing of one clause with its counterpart is a sign that it hits the truth and reality, and that it is a mark of truthfulness. [Page 34]

Sufyan described it with his hand: he tilted it and spread the fingers of his right hand, placing some above others. The eavesdropper hears the word and throws it to the one beneath him, then that one throws it to the one beneath him, until it is cast onto the tongue of the soothsayer or the sorcerer. Sometimes the shooting star overtakes the listener before he casts it, and sometimes he casts it before it overtakes him, and he lies with it a hundred lies. He expressed it by "hearing" because it ultimately returns to news. What the eavesdropper obtains is the awareness of what the angels are directed to accomplish, and what the soothsayer obtains is likewise. The outcome is that the soothsayer reports it, and so it returns to something heard.

[p. 28]

When the preceding discourse concerning the disbelief of the polytheists in the message of Muhammad (ﷺ), and what they did in that regard, had run its course, and the foundational principles upon which they built the edifice of their denial were two, namely his refutation of the divinity of their idols and his affirmation of the Resurrection, the Qur'an set out to show them the proofs that God Most High alone is divine. It mentioned the clear proofs from the creation of the heavens and the earth. It then followed them with proofs of the possibility of resurrection from the creation of life and death and the extinction of nations. It followed these with other proofs in His words, Most High, ﴿And indeed, it is We who give life and cause death, and We are the inheritors﴾ [al-Hijr 15:23], and so on. This coincided with the mention of the opening of the gates of heaven in depicting their arrogance in their obstinacy, so the transition to it was a masterful digression (takhallus).

Within this there is a form of argument against their obstinacy, for if they had sought the truth, the evidence in what is from them would have sufficed them, without seeking supernatural marvels.

The report (khabar) is used for reminder and argument, because the meaning of these reports is known to them.

[p. 29]

The discourse opens with the lam of oath and the particle of emphasis (harf al-tahqiq), treating the addressees, who are heedless of drawing this inference, as if they were in doubt. So the discourse is reinforced for them with two emphasizers. The purpose of the emphasis returns to confirming the argument and compelling them to acknowledge it.

Al-burūj (the constellations, sing. burj, with a dammah on the b) literally means a large building built for dwelling or for fortification, and it is synonymous with a palace. God Most High said: ﴿Even if you were in towers built up high﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:78], in Surat al-Nisa'.

The term burj was applied to a specific area in the apparent position of a group of non-wandering stars (the fixed stars), some of which are clustered near one another at fixed distances that do not change as observed in the sky. That group forms a single shape resembling dots which, if lines were drawn between them, would produce something like the image of an animal or an instrument. They named those stars after the likeness of that shape, and they lie along the path of the sun's course.

The early astronomers of timekeeping (al-tawqit) named them with terms synonymous with "house" or "place." The Arabs called them burūj and dārāt by way of a metaphor that became the cause of the naming. They imagined that they were the stations of the sun, because they fixed the time by its direction, that is, the position of the sun in the vault of the sky by day, as it appears to the observer that the sun travels in something like an arc of a circle. They made them twelve stations, corresponding to the number of the months of the solar year. In reality, they are nothing but the directions of regions, each of which faces the earth from a side beyond the sun for a specific period. Then, when the earth's position changes in its orbit each month of the year, the region facing it changes. By the order that exists in them, it became possible to make them signs marking the times when the four seasons and the twelve months arrive. So they fixed for these signs imaginary boundaries, whose places they determined at night by reference to the position of the sun in the day. They repeated the observation day after day. Whenever a month of the year had passed, they fixed for the following month signs in the region facing the sun's position in that period, and so on, until after twelve months they saw that they had returned to the region facing the point from which they had started. So they made that a complete year. The path that the sun is imagined to have traversed during the year they called the circle of the burūj or the zodiac belt. To distinguish these groups of stars from one another, they gave them names of the things to which they likened them, and they added the word burj to them.

[p. 30 is not reached yet; continuing from p. 29]

The order of these is, starting from the constellation of the entry of the spring season: al-Hamal (Aries), al-Thawr (Taurus), al-Jawza' (Gemini), derived from al-jawz, with a fatha and a sukun on the middle letter, because it lies across the middle of the sky; al-Saratan (Cancer), al-Asad (Leo), al-Sunbula (Virgo), al-Mizan (Libra), al-'Aqrab (Scorpio), al-Qaws (Sagittarius), al-Jady (Capricorn), al-Dalw (Aquarius), al-Hut (Pisces).

For the constellation of Aries they took the month of April, and so on. This happened by coincidence, in that the sun at that time was in the direction of a star-shaped figure that they likened to the dotted outline of the image of a ram. On this basis it is believed that the ancients fixed the solar year and divided it into the four seasons and the twelve months before they fixed the constellations. They only fixed the constellations to specify the timing of the beginnings of the seasons, so that they might know how much of their duration had passed and how much remained.

The first to draw these figures were the Chaldeans (al-Kaldaniyyun), and then their knowledge passed to the rest of the nations, among them the Arabs, who knew them, fixed them, and named them in their own language.

For this reason the Qur'an made the constellations a proof of His great power and His sole creation, because they knew their fine details and the order by which they were prepared, in order to serve as a means of fixing times in such a way that the observation of their observer is never mistaken. God did not create them in that condition except so that they would be suited to fixing times, as God Most High said: ﴿so that you may know the number of years and the reckoning﴾ [Yunus 10:5]. Then it advanced in the argument by noting that these great constellations were made in shapes that are pleasing to the eye, so they were an adornment for those who look, who enjoy beholding them at night. Thus their benefits are numerous.

As for His words, ﴿and We guarded them from every accursed devil﴾, this is an insertion of instruction within the course of the argument. In it there is an affirmation of the infallibility (ismah) of revelation from being subject to addition or subtraction,

[p. 30]

namely that the realms from which revelation descends and in which it travels are preserved from the corrupt elements. It is linked to His words, ﴿and indeed We are its guardians﴾ [al-Hijr 15:9].

For this reason al-Walid ibn al-Mughira said, when he debated with them about the excuses they had prepared for the delegations of the Arabs during the pilgrimage season, should they ask them about this man who claimed prophethood, and they had proposed to say: "He is a soothsayer." Among al-Walid's words was that he said: ". . . No, by God, he is not a soothsayer. The earth – We spread it out, cast into it firm mountains, and caused to grow in it every thing in due measure. And We made for you therein means of livelihood, and [also] for those whom you do not provide for.

This is a transition from reasoning through the heavenly signs to reasoning through the earthly signs, due to the relation of contrast (al-muḍādda).

The discussion of the meaning of "madadnāhā" (We spread it out) and of "al-rawāsī" (the firm mountains) has already been given in Surat al-Ra'd.

"Al-mawzūn" (in due measure): used metaphorically for that which is fixed and precisely regulated.

"Ma'āyish" (means of livelihood): the plural of "ma'īshah," and after the alif there is a yā' (ي), not a hamzah, as was explained at the beginning of Surat al-A'rāf.

"Wa man lastum lahu bi-rāziqīn" (and for those whom you do not provide for): this is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) on the pronoun in "lakum" (for you). For conjoining upon a separate pronoun in the genitive case, it is not necessary, according to the verified view, to separate it with a separate pronoun. The meaning is: We made for you, O addressees, means of livelihood on the earth, and We made on the earth means of livelihood for those whom you do not provide for, i.e., for those for whom you are not the providers of food.

The referent of "man" (those) is that which eats of its food from what is on the earth, namely the creatures that subsist on the plants of the earth, and whom people do not perceive (as provided for by them).

The use of "man," which is predominantly used for rational beings, is for the purpose of prevailing (al-taghlīb) of the rational.

The meaning of "lastum lahu bi-rāziqīn" is a negation that you are its providers; for "al-rizq" means providing food. The verbal noun of "razaqahu" is "al-razq" with a fatḥah on the rā'. As for "al-rizq" with a kasrah on the rā', it is the noun, and it means sustenance (al-qūt).
