Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 15, verse 21:

[Page 36]
﴿And there is not a thing but that with Us are its treasuries, and We do not send it down except in a known measure.﴾

This is an interjection (i'tiraḍ) arising from His saying ﴿And We caused to grow therein of every thing weighed⁠﴾ [al-Ḥijr: 19], and it is a tadhyil (a concluding sentence that reinforces the preceding statement).

By "thing" (shay') is meant that which is beneficial to people, by the indication of His saying ﴿And We caused to grow therein of every thing weighed⁠﴾ [al-Ḥijr: 19] and what follows. In the speech there is an ellipsis of the qualifier, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿who seizes every boat by force⁠﴾ [al-Kahf: 79], meaning: every sound boat.

The "treasuries" (khazā'in) is a metaphor (tamthil) for the readiness of the divine power to bring into being beneficial things. The manner of bringing beneficial things into existence is likened to the manner of bringing stored goods out of storehouses, in the form of a metaphorical allegory (al-tamthiliyya al-makniyya). The likened form is indicated by one of its necessary attributes, namely "treasuries." This was already discussed at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Say: I do not tell you that with me are the treasuries of God⁠﴾ [al-An'am: 50], in Surat al-An'am.

This includes the scattered things in the world that reach people through impulses and causes that are established under particular circumstances, or through the combination of one thing with another, such as the descent of hail from the clouds and the gushing of springs from the earth, whether by intention or by chance.

As for His saying ﴿and We do not send it down except in a known measure⁠﴾, "sending down" (inzal) is applied to enabling people to use the things that God created for their benefit. He, exalted is He, said ﴿It is He who created for you all that is on the earth⁠﴾ [al-Baqara: 29], in Surat al-Baqara. This is a figurative usage, because what God created, being an effect of the divine command of creation, is likened, in enabling people to have it, to the sending down of something from a height, by considering that it belongs to the transcendent (ladunni) world, which is a figurative height. Or by considering that the disposal of affairs takes place in the higher worlds. This is like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And He sent down for you eight pairs of livestock⁠﴾ [al-Zumar: 6], in Surat al-Zumar, and His saying, exalted is He, ﴿The command descends among them⁠﴾ [al-Talaq: 12], in Surat al-Talaq.

[Page 37]
Al-qadar, with a fatḥa on the dal, means determination (taqdir). It was discussed at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿so the valleys flowed according to their measure⁠﴾ [al-Ra'd: 17], in Surat al-Ra'd.
What is meant by it is "known," meaning that its determined measure is known to God, exalted is He.

[p. 38]

This is a transition from reasoning based on the apparent features of the sky and the earth to reasoning based on the apparent features of the sphere of air that lies between the sky and the earth. It is for reflection on the action of the winds and the favour of what they contain of benefits.

"Irsal" (sending) is a figurative usage (*majaz*) for moving something from one place to another. This indicates that the winds blow continuously in the air sphere, arriving in one place from another, and so on. . .

*Lawaqih* is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) modifying "the winds." This circumstance came as an *idmaj* (incorporation, combining two meanings in one expression) to convey two meanings, as will come from Malik, may Allah have mercy on him.

*Lawaqih* may be the plural of *laqih*, meaning a pregnant she-camel. It is used here as a metaphor for the wind that contains moisture, which is the cause of the descent of rain. Likewise, its opposite, *'aqim* (barren), the opposite of *laqih*, is used in His saying, ﴿When We sent upon them the barren wind﴾ [adh-Dhariyat: 41].

It may also be the plural of *mulaqqih*, meaning one that makes another pregnant, i.e., the stallion when it impregnates the she-camel. The form *fawa'il* comes as the plural of *mif'il* (masculine) rarely, as in the words of al-Harith or Dirar al-Nahshali:

*Labbayka Yazid, a suppliant for a dispute, and one who gropes for what the falling calamities bring down.*

Here, the feminine plural was observed for the thing compared (*al-mushabbah bihi*), which is the plural of stallions, because the plural of non-rational beings may be treated as feminine.

The meaning of *ilqah* (impregnation) is that the winds impregnate the clouds with water, by directing the alternating action of heat and cold. From this arises vapour, which becomes water in the atmosphere, then descends as rain upon the earth. And they impregnate fruit-bearing trees by carrying to their blossoms a fine dust from the pollen of the male tree, so that its fruit becomes sound or sets; without this, it does not set or does not become sound. This is *al-ibar* (pollination). Some of it is not achieved except by hanging the male spathe on the fruit-bearing tree, and some of it is sufficient by planting a male tree among the fruit trees.

Among the eloquence of the verse is the mention of this attribute to convey both actions that the winds perform. The verse has been interpreted with both, but the majority of exegetes have limited themselves to the meaning that the winds impregnate the clouds with rain.

Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi related from Malik that he said: "Allah the Exalted said, ﴿And We sent the winds fertilizing﴾. So the impregnation of wheat, in my view, is that it becomes grainy and ears up, and I do not mean what dries up in its husks, but that it becomes grainy so that, if it dried at that time, it would not be corruption without any good in it. And the impregnation of all trees is that they bear fruit, then some of it falls and some of it remains."

The consequence of His saying ﴿So We sent down from the sky water﴾ is upon His saying ﴿And We sent the winds﴾.

Hamza recited (*wa arsalna ar-rih lawaqih*) with the singular *ar-rih* and the plural *lawaqih*, intending the genus, and the genus has several individuals.

*Asqaynakumuhu* means "We made it for you as drink (*suqya*)," so the *hamza* in it indicates making. The use of *asqa* in the sense of *saqa* is common.

Here *al-khazn* (storing) is used in the same sense as His saying just before, ﴿And there is nothing but that with Us are its treasuries﴾ [al-Hijr: 21]. That is: "And you are not those who keep it safe or produce it whenever you wish."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 15, verse 23:

﴿And indeed, it is We who give life and cause death, and We are the Inheritors.﴾ When the mention of the sending down of rain had passed, and among what comes readily to mind at the mention of rain is the giving of life to the earth through it, it was appropriate that after it there be mentioned the whole category of giving life, because of what it contains of the purpose of reasoning for those heedless of the Oneness (tawhid); and because in it is evidence for the possibility of resurrection (al-ba'th). The intended matter is the mention of giving life, and for this reason He placed causing death first, for completeness (li-l-takmil).

The sentence is coordinated (ʿatf) upon the sentence ﴿And We have placed in the sky constellations﴾ [al-Hijr: 16], to indicate power and the comprehensiveness of control (tasarruf).

The pronoun "naḥnu" is a pronoun of separation (ḍamir al-faṣl), upon which the lam of initiation (lam al-ibtida') has entered. The predicate is emphasized by "inna" (indeed), the lam, and the pronoun of separation, for its confirmation, and in order to place those addressed, in their associating others with God, in the position of those who deny giving life and causing death.

By "giving life" is meant the bringing into existence of beings in which there is life, and their being given life again after the bodies have perished. In the proof of God the Exalted's sole control, the affirmation of resurrection and the repelling of the assumption that it is unlikely to occur or impossible has been incorporated (udmija).

Since the polytheists were deniers of giving life, the emphasis of the predicate was used in both its literal (haqiqi) and its figurative/ascriptive (tanzili) senses.

The sentence ﴿and We are the Inheritors﴾ is coordinated upon the sentence "And indeed We give life and cause death."

The meaning of inheritance (al-irth) here is remaining after the existing things, by way of analogy with inheritance, which is the taking of what the deceased leaves of land and other things.

[Page 40]

﴿And We have certainly known those of you who go ahead, and We have certainly known those who come later.﴾ ﴿Indeed, your Lord—it is He who will gather them. Indeed, He is All-Wise, All-Knowing.﴾

When He mentioned giving life and causing death, and "giving life" (al-iḥyāʾ, with a kasra on the hamza) reminds one of "the living" (al-aḥyāʾ, with a fatḥa on the hamza), and causing death is mentioned with the dead who have passed away, he moved from the proof of His great power through giving life and causing death to a proof of what necessarily follows from that, namely His great knowledge, which is His knowledge of the nations that have perished and His knowledge of the nations that are present. So by "those who go ahead" (al-mustaqdimīn) is meant those who have gone ahead of the living toward death or toward the Hereafter; thus "going ahead" (al-taqaddum) here carries the sense of having passed on. By "those who come later" (al-mustaʾkhirīn) is meant those who lag behind, who come after the others have died out, until an appointed term that is yet to come.

The sīn and tāʾ in the two descriptive forms are for emphasis, as in istajāba (he answered). However, their saying istaqdama in the sense of taqaddama (he went ahead) is contrary to analogy (ʿalā khilāf al-qiyās), because its verb is quadriliteral (rubāʿī). This was discussed under His saying, exalted is He, ﴿They cannot delay an hour, nor can they advance﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 34], in Surat al-Aʿrāf.

Already mentioned at the opening of the tafsīr (exegesis) of this surah is the report that al-Tirmidhī recorded in his Jāmiʿ through the chain of Nūḥ ibn Qays and through the chain of Jaʿfar ibn Sulaymān concerning the occasion of revelation of this verse. It is a weak report (khabar wāhin) which does not accord with the coherence of the verses, and it can only come from weak exegetical works (al-tafāsīr al-ḍaʿīfa).

The clause ﴿Indeed, your Lord—it is He who will gather them﴾ is the conclusion (natīja) of these proofs from His saying, ﴿Indeed, it is We who give life and cause death﴾ [al-Ḥijr: 23]. For He who gives the first life is able to give the second life all the more so, and He who decreed death did not decree it in vain after He brought existing things into being, but so that you would face an everlasting life. Had it not been so, permanence in the first life would have been decreed. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿He who created death and life that He may test you as to which of you is best in deed﴾ [al-Mulk: 2].

To point to this meaning from the wisdom of giving life and causing death, He followed it with His saying, ﴿Indeed, He is All-Wise, All-Knowing﴾, as a justification (taʿlīl) for the clause ﴿Indeed, your Lord—it is He who will gather them﴾. This is because the nature of inna, when it comes in a sense other than refuting a denier, is to convey the meaning of causal justification and connection with what precedes it.

[Page 41]

Al-Ḥakīm (the All-Wise) is the one described with wisdom (al-ḥikma). This was discussed under His saying, ﴿He gives wisdom to whom He wills﴾ [al-Baqara: 269], and under His saying, ﴿Know that Allah is Mighty, All-Wise﴾ [al-Baqara: 209], in Surat al-Baqara.

Al-ʿAlīm (the All-Knowing) is the one described with comprehensive knowledge, that is, the all-encompassing. This was discussed under His saying, ﴿And that Allah may know those who believe﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 140], in Surat Āl ʿImrān.

The clause ﴿Indeed, your Lord—it is He who will gather them﴾ has been emphasized with the particle of emphasis and with the pronoun of separation (ḍamīr al-faṣl), in response to their intense denial of the gathering (al-ḥashr). The gathering has been attributed to Allah under the title of His being the Lord of Muhammad ﷺ, as an honouring of the status of the Prophet ﷺ. This is because they denied him in what he reported about resurrection. And those who disbelieved said: "Shall we direct you to a man who will tell you that when you are completely torn apart, you will be in a new creation? Has he invented a lie against Allah, or is there madness in him?" That is: how, then, do you think will be the requital of those who deny you when He gathers them?

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 15, verse 26–27:

﴿And We certainly created man from clay, from black mud altered in form.﴾ ﴿And the jinn We had created before, from the fire of scorching wind.﴾ This is a supplement to establishing the proof of His, the Exalted's, sole creation of the kinds of worlds and what is in them. From it he transitions to reminding of the enmity of Satan towards mankind, so that they may take their precaution against him and hold themselves accountable for what his whisperings insinuate into them that would ruin them. It comes in connection with the mention of giving life and causing death; for the most important form of giving life is the bringing into existence of the human species. In this report there is therefore an argument for the greatness of power and wisdom, and for the possibility of resurrection, as well as an admonition and a reminder. The intended "man" is Adam (peace be upon him).

Al-ṣalṣāl (ṣalṣāl): clay that is left until it dries; when it has dried it is ṣalṣāl, and it is similar to fakhkhār (pottery), except that fakhkhār is what has dried by firing in fire. The Exalted said: ﴿He created man from clay like pottery﴾ [al-Rahman: 14].

Page 42

Al-ḥama' (ḥama'): mud when it has blackened and its smell has become disagreeable. The phrase min ḥama' is an attribute of ṣalṣāl, and masnūn is an attribute of ḥama' or of ṣalṣāl. Since ṣalṣāl is from ḥama', the attribute of one of them is an attribute of the other. Al-masnūn: that which has remained for a long duration; it is an ism maf'ūl from the verb sannahu, when he left it for a long period resembling a year (sanah). I suppose that the verb (sanna) meaning "to leave something for a long duration" is not attested.

Perhaps (tasannah), meaning "to change due to the length of time," originates from the reflexive form (muṭāwi') of sanah, then the meaning of reflexivity was forgotten from it. The Exalted's saying ﴿lam yatasannah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 259] has already been mentioned in Surat al-Baqarah.

The purpose of mentioning these things is to draw attention to the wondrous craftsmanship of God, the Exalted, when He brings out of this humble state a kind that is the lord of the kinds of the world of matter possessing life.

In this there is an indication that the reality of life is constituted from earthiness, moisture and putrefaction, and it gives off weak heat; for this reason creatures such as worms arise in putrefying bodies, and for this reason too fevers arise in putrefying temperaments.

In this there is an indication of the stages through which the material of human creation passed.

The emphasis of the sentence with the oath-particle lam and the particle (qad) is for increased certainty, drawing attention to the importance of this creation and that it is in this manner.

The conjunction of the sentence ﴿wa-l-jānna khalaqnāhu﴾ is an idmāj (incorporation) and a preparation for explaining the origin of the enmity between Adam and the hosts of Iblis. The sentence "wa-l-jānna khalaqnāhu" was emphasized with the construction of ishtighāl (the verb-object construction with a pronoun), which strengthens the verb by implying a counterpart of the elided element, and because of the concern it contains with the summary followed by the detail, for the same purpose for which the sentence ﴿wa-laqad khalaqnā al-insān﴾ etc. was emphasized.

Page 43

The benefit of his saying min qablu, i.e., from before the creation of man, is to teach that the creation of the jinn is prior, because it was created from the element of heat, which precedes moisture.

Al-samūm, with a fatḥah on the sīn: the scorching wind. So the jinn were created from fire and wind, so that moderation in heat is achieved and it accepts the special life suitable to the creation of the jinn. Just as God formed the black mud, the clay that is masnūn, for the creation of man, so He formed a scorching wind and made the jinn from it. Thus it is formed from heat exceeding the measure of human heat and from a strong ventilation, and the wisdom lies entirely in the perfection of the mixing and composition.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 15, verse 28–35:

﴿And when your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed, I will create a human being from clay, from black mud altered in form."﴾ ﴿So when I have proportioned him and breathed into him of My [created] soul, fall down to him in prostration.﴾ ﴿So the angels prostrated, all of them entirely,﴾ ﴿except Iblees; he refused to be among those who prostrate.﴾ ﴿[Allah] said, "O Iblees, what is [the matter] with you that you are not among those who prostrate?"﴾ ﴿He said, "I would never prostrate to a human whom You created from clay from black mud altered in form."﴾ ﴿[Allah] said, "Then get out of it, for indeed, you are expelled.﴾ ﴿And indeed, upon you is the curse until the Day of Recompense."﴾

This is the conjunction of one narrative upon another narrative.

"Idh" (when) is an object of a deleted verb "udhkur" (remember), and the discussion of its like has preceded in Surat al-Baqarah and Surat al-A'raf.

"Al-Basharu" (the human being) is a synonym of "al-Insan" (the human), meaning: "Indeed, I will create a human." The angels understood the reality through what Allah placed in them of knowledge, or Allah described to them the reality of the human being in the sense that was expressed in the Qur'an with a comprehensive phrase for that meaning.

Page 44
He mentioned to the angels the material from which the human was created only so that they would know that the honour of created beings lies in their qualities, not in the material of their composition, as His saying ﴿So when I have proportioned him and breathed into him of My [created] soul, fall down to him in prostration﴾ alludes to that.
"Taswiyah" (proportioning) is the modification of the essence of a thing, and it is used here for the balance of the elements in it and their completion such that it becomes receptive to the breathing of the soul.

"Nafkh" (breathing) in its literal sense is the expulsion of air compressed between two closed lips, like whistling, and it is borrowed here for placing a power that is subtle in its spread and strong in its effect, all at once, and there is no blowing nor a thing blown.

An approximation of the breathing of the soul into the living being is that there occurs the vaporous or electrical power emanating from the heart when the balance of temperament is complete and the components of the temperament are combined, a sudden rapid formation, and the effects of that power flow through the channels of the arteries to the depths of the body, into the cavities of all its principal and other organs.

The attribution of the breathing and the addition of the soul to the pronoun of the Name of Majesty is an honouring of this creature, and in it is an allusion that the realities of the elements in the sight of Allah Most High are not differentiated except by the differentiation of their effects and actions, and that the disliking of a substance or a smell to a state that some people or all of them dislike is only following what suits or repels the sensory perception, according to the natures of temperaments or the habituation of custom, and it is not given consideration in the knowledge of Allah Most High. This is the criterion of the description of filth and purity among human beings.

Do you not see that semen is found repugnant by human sense, although from it is the formation of its kind, and from it were created the best of human beings; and likewise musk is pleasant to human sense because its fragrance suits the smell, and it is nothing but a gland from the secretions of some kinds of gazelle. Allah Most High said ﴿And He began the creation of man from clay﴾ [As-Sajdah: 7] ﴿Then He made his descendants from an extract of fluid, [from] a disdained liquid﴾ [As-Sajdah: 8] ﴿Then He proportioned him and breathed into him of His soul and made for you hearing and sight and hearts; little are you grateful﴾ [As-Sajdah: 9].

Page 45

His saying ﴿to a human whom You created from clay from black mud altered in form﴾ is a reinforcement of his refusal to prostrate, on the ground that what is created from that clay is base and despicable and does not deserve prostration. This is the conjunction of one narrative upon another narrative.

"Nafkh" (breathing) in its literal sense is the expulsion of air compressed between two closed lips, like whistling, and it is borrowed here for placing a power that is subtle in its spread and strong in its effect, all at once, and there is no blowing nor a thing blown.

An approximation of the breathing of the soul into the living being is that there occurs the vaporous or electrical power emanating from the heart when the balance of temperament is complete and the components of the temperament are combined, a sudden rapid formation, and the effects of that power flow through the channels of the arteries to the depths of the body, into the cavities of all its principal and other organs.

The attribution of the breathing and the addition of the soul to the pronoun of the Name of Majesty is an honouring of this creature, and in it is an allusion that the realities of the elements in the sight of Allah Most High are not differentiated except by the differentiation of their effects and actions, and that the disliking of a substance or a smell to a state that some people or all of them dislike is only following what suits or repels the sensory perception, according to the natures of temperaments or the habituation of custom, and it is not given consideration in the knowledge of Allah Most High. This is the criterion of the description of filth and purity among human beings.

Do you not see that semen is found repugnant by human sense, although from it is the formation of its kind, and from it were created the best of human beings; and likewise musk is pleasant to human sense because its fragrance suits the smell, and it is nothing but a gland from the secretions of some kinds of gazelle. Allah Most High said ﴿And He began the creation of man from clay﴾ [As-Sajdah: 7] ﴿Then He made his descendants from an extract of fluid, [from] a disdained liquid﴾ [As-Sajdah: 8] ﴿Then He proportioned him and breathed into him of His soul and made for you hearing and sight and hearts; little are you grateful﴾ [As-Sajdah: 9].

[Page 48]

His request for respite, after being told that he is cursed until the Day of Judgment, was prompted by the extreme wickedness of his nature, which is not cured except by the continuation of corruption in this world. Thus this desire brought about the continuation of his misery.

Since a curse continues even after the cursed person has ceased to exist, if his evil is well known among people, then fixing its duration as "forever" does not restrict the life of the cursed one. For this reason, Iblis had no need, from God's words "until the Day of Judgment," to ask to be kept alive until the Day of Judgment, so that he could be the source of evils for souls, in fulfillment of what he was created with, namely the spreading of wickedness. Thus he was eager for its continuation, through the curse directed at him, so he asked for respite out of love for remaining alive, because in continued existence his work continues.

He addressed God with the attribute of lordship (rububiyyah), displaying humility and urging a response. The "fa" in "fa-anzirni" is the fa of consequence (tafri'), meaning that he based his request on the expulsion, and he placed the address (nida') in between.

This state has been mentioned among the descriptions of his self, to arouse aversion to him in the hearts of humans, who regard it as the nature of a noble soul to recoil from a base and despised life. This is the disposition of the Arabs. When they learn of this baseness in Iblis's condition, they hate him and despise him, and they do not approve of any action attributed to him.

Al-inzar means granting respite and delay. It has been discussed in His words, ﴿then let there be postponement until a time of ease﴾ [al-Baqarah: 280], in Surat al-Baqarah. The intended meaning here is the delay of his death, because respite cannot apply to the essence itself, so it is determined to refer to one of its states, which is death, by the indication of the context.

He expressed the Day of Judgment as "the Day they are raised" as a preparation for what he had resolved upon concerning the misguidance of humans. So he wanted respite until the last period of the existence of the human species in this world. God created in him the love of respite, which God had decreed for him and created him for, and for its effects, so that he would bear the burden of its consequences through his own earning and choice of that state. For that earning and choice is what makes him suited to what he was created for. This is what the prophetic statement indicates: "Each is made easy for that for which he was created."

The pronoun in "yub'athun" refers to the humans known from the composition of the creation of Adam (peace be upon him), and that he would have offspring, especially since his wife was created at that time, which requires that offspring come from the two of them.

He expressed the Day of Resurrection as ﴿the day of the appointed time﴾ as a stylistic variation, avoiding repetition of the word, fulfilling the requirement of fine composition, and also because it teaches that Allah knows that term. So the meaning is "known to Us." It is also possible that the meaning is "known to people" as well, with general knowledge.

In this there is an implicit indication that those among people who do not believe in that Day are not regarded; they are as nothing.

This respite is a divine symbol that the law of evil does not end in the life of this world, and that its order rests on the struggle between good and evil, and between the righteous and the wicked. God said: ﴿Rather, We hurl the truth against falsehood﴾ [al-Anbiya': 18], and He said: ﴿Thus Allah strikes [examples of] truth and falsehood﴾ [al-Ra'd: 17]. Therefore the order of the world does not dispense with establishing the laws of justice and righteousness and entrusting them to capable guardians to implement them and defend them.

The statements of these sayings are joined by "fa" because each statement was prompted by the preceding discourse, and so it branches from it.

﴿He said, "My Lord, because You have led me astray, I will certainly make [evil] seem attractive to them on earth and will certainly lead them all astray,"﴾ ﴿"except for Your chosen servants among them."﴾

The *ba'* in *bima ughwaytani* is causal (*lil-sababiyyah*), and *ma* is a relative pronoun (*mawsulah*). The meaning is: "because of your leading me astray," that is, "because you created me as one who goes astray, so I will lead mankind astray."

The *lam* in *la-uzayyinanna* is the *lam* of an oath (*lam qasam*) whose oath particle is omitted, and it is meant for emphasis. The explicit oath appears in His words, ﴿He said, "By Your might, I will certainly lead them all astray,"﴾ [Sad 38:82].

[p. 50]

*Tazyin* means embellishment (*tahsin*): making a thing adorned (*zayn*), that is, good. The object of *la-uzayyinanna* is omitted because it is clear from context. The meaning is: "I will certainly make evil and misdeeds seem good to them, so they will see them as good, and I will make attractive to them the pursuit of pleasures that will distract them from their obligations." Its discussion occurred earlier at His words, ﴿The life of this world was made attractive to those who disbelieve﴾ in Surat al-Baqarah.

*Al-ighwa'* means causing them to be astray (*ghawin*). *Al-ghawayah*, with a fatha on the *ghayn*, means misguidance (*al-dalal*).

The meaning is: "I will certainly lead them astray." Leading all people astray is the highest degree of the misleader's aims, since his misguidance extends to bringing about the misguidance of others.

From this it is known that His words, *bima ughwaytani*, refer to a misguidance known to God, which is the disposition He fashioned in him. Therefore the relative construction was chosen to report it. It is also known that this statement of Satan is an outpouring of what is in his nature, and not a matter of seeking revenge or provoking anger, because divine majesty restrains him from that.

The addition of *fi al-ard* ("on earth") is because it is the first thing that comes to his mind when the thought of misguidance arises, since misguidance is linked with descent to the earth, which is indicated by His words, ﴿So get out of it﴾, that is, get out of the Garden to the earth, as in the other verse, ﴿He said, "Go down, some of you enemies to others, and for you on earth is a dwelling place."﴾ Also, making the embellishment "on earth" conveys that it spreads to everything on the earth, its beings and their conditions.

The pronouns in *lahum*, *la-ughwiyannahum* and *minhum* refer to the children of Adam, because he knew, through knowledge placed in his awareness, that Adam, upon him be peace, would have descendants; or he acquired that knowledge from reports of the higher world during the time he was among its people and its company.

He made those who are led astray the primary category and made an exception of God's chosen servants, because his resolve is directed toward misguidance, so it is what is initially in view for him. Moreover, those who are led astray are the majority. The opposite is His words, ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them, except those who follow you.﴾ An exception does not imply that the excepted group is small relative to the group from which it is excepted, nor the reverse.

[p. 51]

*Al-ighwa'* means causing them to be astray (*ghawin*). *Al-ghawayah*, with a fatha on the *ghayn*, means misguidance (*al-dalal*).

The meaning is: "I will certainly lead them astray." Leading all people astray is the highest degree of the misleader's aims, since his misguidance extends to bringing about the misguidance of others.

From this it is known that His words, *bima ughwaytani*, refer to a misguidance known to God, which is the disposition He fashioned in him. Therefore the relative construction was chosen to report it. It is also known that this statement of Satan is an outpouring of what is in his nature, and not a matter of seeking revenge or provoking anger, because divine majesty restrains him from that.

The addition of *fi al-ard* ("on earth") is because it is the first thing that comes to his mind when the thought of misguidance arises, since misguidance is linked with descent to the earth, which is indicated by His words, ﴿So get out of it﴾, that is, get out of the Garden to the earth, as in the other verse, ﴿He said, "Go down, some of you enemies to others, and for you on earth is a dwelling place."﴾ Also, making the embellishment "on earth" conveys that it spreads to everything on the earth, its beings and their conditions.

The pronouns in *lahum*, *la-ughwiyannahum* and *minhum* refer to the children of Adam, because he knew, through knowledge placed in his awareness, that Adam, upon him be peace, would have descendants; or he acquired that knowledge from reports of the higher world during the time he was among its people and its company.

He made those who are led astray the primary category and made an exception of God's chosen servants, because his resolve is directed toward misguidance, so it is what is initially in view for him. Moreover, those who are led astray are the majority. The opposite is His words, ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them, except those who follow you.﴾ An exception does not imply that the excepted group is small relative to the group from which it is excepted, nor the reverse.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 15, verses 41–44:**

﴿He said, "This is a straight path upon Me."﴾ ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them, except those who follow you of the deviators.﴾ ﴿And indeed, Hell is the promised place for them all.﴾ ﴿It has seven gates; for each gate there is a designated portion of them.﴾ *al-Sirat al-mustaqim* (the straight path): it is the good and right guidance.

The reference (*al-ishara*) is to what is understood from the sentence that follows the demonstrative noun (*ism al-ishara*), which explains it, namely the sentence "Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them." The demonstrative therefore refers to something not present, treating it as if it were present, and treating what is heard as if it were seen.

Moreover, this thing treated as present is nonetheless not mentioned explicitly, in order to arouse eagerness to hear it when it is mentioned. Thus the demonstrative here functions like the pronoun of the matter (*damir al-sha'n*), as is written in deeds and contracts: "This is what so-and-so has agreed with so-and-so, that he is such and such," or "This is what so-and-so bought from so-and-so, that he sold him such and such."

It is also possible that the reference is to the exception (*al-istithna'*) that preceded in the quotation of Iblis's speech, from his words, "except Your sincere servants among them." This implies that he cannot lead astray the servants whom God has purified for good. In that case, the sentence "Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them" is a new independent statement (*jumla mustanafa'a*), conveying the negation of his authority.

*Al-sirat* is used metaphorically for the course of action by which its doer intends a benefit. It is likened to the road leading to the desired destination, reaching it. That is, "this is the practice that I have established among people, and in your leading them astray: that you lead astray only those who follow you of the deviators, or that you lead astray whoever is other than My sincere servants."

*Mustaqim* is an attributive adjective of *sirat*, meaning that there is no crookedness in it. Straightness is used metaphorically for the constant maintenance of a perfect state.

The particle *'ala* (upon) is used in the figurative sense of obligation, which is a constant act that does not fail, as in His saying, ﴿Indeed, upon Us is the guidance﴾ (Qur'an 92:12), meaning: We have committed Ourselves to guidance and do not deviate from it, because it is required by wisdom and the majesty of divinity.

This sentence is one of the Qur'anic proverbs (*amthal*) that are used as general maxims.

The majority of readers read *'Aliyya* with a fathah on the *lam* and a fathah on the *ya'*, so that *'ala* is joined with the first person pronoun suffix *ya'* (my). Ya'qub read it with a kasrah on the *lam*, a dammah on the *ya'*, and with tanwin, taking it as an adjective derived from *'uluww* (height), applied to *sirat*, meaning: a path of noble and great rank.

The meaning is that God established a practice in human souls: that Satan has no power over anyone except one who is already deviant, that is, inclined to deviation and acquiring it, unlike one who restrains his soul from evil. When a rational person is afflicted by Satan's whispering, he knows the misguidance in it, and knows that guidance lies in its opposite. If he is granted success and compels himself to choose guidance, and directs his resolve toward it, he becomes strong against Satan and Satan has no authority over him. But if he inclines toward error, finds it appealing, and chooses to satisfy his desire, he becomes prepared for deviation, and Satan leads him astray, and he goes astray. So *al-ittiba'* (following) is metaphorical, meaning obedience and approval of an opinion, as in His saying, ﴿Follow me, and God will love you﴾ (Qur'an 3:31).

The use of *al-ghawin* (the deviators) is an application of the active participle to what will occur in the future, indicated by context. For if he were already deviant in act, the authority of Satan over him would serve no purpose. This meaning is indicated by the fact that the negation of authority is attached to all the servants, followed by the exception of those who were deviant. Since Satan's authority has power only over one who is deviant, we know that there is a quality of deviation which prepares the ground for Satan's authority over the one who bears it. That is the one characterized by deviation in potential, not in actual occurrence, that is, by readiness for deviation rather than its actual happening.

Therefore, the annexation in His saying, ﴿My servants﴾, is general, as is the case with a definite plural made definite by annexation. The exception is genuine (*haqiqi*), and there is no difficulty in this.

The pronoun in *mawid-uhum* refers to "those who follow you." *Al-mawid* is the place of promise. Here it is applied to the return to God, and *al-mawid* is used metaphorically for the place of meeting, likening it to a specific place fixed among people for a specific meeting, which is the promise.

The point of resemblance is the certainty of arrival, with the common element being the eagerness for it, which is the nature of promises, since breaking a promise is to be avoided. In this there is an allusion (*tamlih*) to them, because they deny resurrection and recompense. Thus they are placed in the position of one who has set that place for coming.

The sentence ﴿It has seven gates﴾ is an independent sentence describing the state of Hell and its gates, in order to prepare people so that it will not be too narrow for their entry.

The apparent meaning is that the number seven is used for multiplicity, as in His saying, ﴿and the angels will enter upon them from every gate﴾ (Qur'an 13:23). Or the gates are intended as a metonymy (*kinaya*) for the levels (*tabaqat*) of Hell, because gates imply dwellings, so they are ranks corresponding to degrees of crime. The essential crimes are seven, from which all the major sins branch out. We may, God willing, be able to trace these branches at another time.

It may be that among its levels is the level of hypocrisy, as He said, ﴿Indeed, the hypocrites will be in the lowest depth of the Fire﴾ (Qur'an 4:145). Consider what we have previously set forth about the branching of what arises from hypocrisy of blameworthy qualities, in His saying, ﴿And among people is one who says, "We believe in God and the Last Day"﴾ (Qur'an 2:8), in Surat al-Baqarah.

The sentence ﴿for each gate there is a designated portion of them﴾ is a description of *abwab* (gates). Its division by specific determination is known to God the Exalted. The pronoun in *minhum* refers to "those who follow you of the deviators," meaning: for each gate there is a group that enters through it, or for each level of the Fire there is a portion of the people of the Fire, apportioned according to the levels of the divisions of the Fire.

Know that these statements that came from Satan in the sacred presence are a disclosure of the innate nature of the development (*tatawwur*) through which the soul of Iblis took form from the time he refused to prostrate, and how each stage of that development emerged from what preceded it, until the satanic essence (*mahiyya*) was completed with its constituent elements, when he said, ﴿I will surely adorn [evil] for them on earth and will surely mislead them all, except Your sincere servants among them﴾ (Qur'an 15:39–40). Whenever a stage of that essence came into being in his nature, a statement came from him indicating it. This is like the testimony of the limbs speaking against the people of error on the Day of Reckoning.

As for the divine statements to which Satan's statements were answered, they manifest the commands of creation (*al-awamir al-takwiniyya*) which God decreed in His knowledge for the development of the stages of Iblis that constitute the reality of Satanhood (*shaytana*), and for the subtle favors which God has decreed for those of His servants who hold fast to them in resisting Satan's authority. Those statements are not all a debate between God and one of His creatures, nor a victory of Satan over his Creator, for his weakness before the might of his Creator does not reach to that.

For if he were already deviant in act, the authority of Satan over him would serve no purpose. This meaning is indicated by the fact that the negation of authority is attached to all the servants, followed by the exception of those who were deviant. Since Satan's authority has power only over one who is deviant, we know that there is a quality of deviation which prepares the ground for Satan's authority over the one who bears it. That is the one characterized by deviation in potential, not in actual occurrence, that is, by readiness for deviation rather than its actual happening.

Therefore, the annexation in His saying, ﴿My servants﴾, is general, as is the case with a definite plural made definite by annexation. The exception is genuine (*haqiqi*), and there is no difficulty in this.

The pronoun in *mawid-uhum* refers to "those who follow you." *Al-mawid* is the place of promise. Here it is applied to the return to God, and *al-mawid* is used metaphorically for the place of meeting, likening it to a specific place fixed among people for a specific meeting, which is the promise.

The point of resemblance is the certainty of arrival, with the common element being the eagerness for it, which is the nature of promises, since breaking a promise is to be avoided. In this there is an allusion (*tamlih*) to them, because they deny resurrection and recompense. Thus they are placed in the position of one who has set that place for coming.

The sentence ﴿It has seven gates﴾ is an independent sentence describing the state of Hell and its gates, in order to prepare people so that it will not be too narrow for their entry.

The apparent meaning is that the number seven is used for multiplicity, as in His saying, ﴿and the angels will enter upon them from every gate﴾ (Qur'an 13:23). Or the gates are intended as a metonymy (*kinaya*) for the levels (*tabaqat*) of Hell, because gates imply dwellings, so they are ranks corresponding to degrees of crime. The essential crimes are seven, from which all the major sins branch out. We may, God willing, be able to trace these branches at another time.

It may be that among its levels is the level of hypocrisy, as He said, ﴿Indeed, the hypocrites will be in the lowest depth of the Fire﴾ (Qur'an 4:145). Consider what we have previously set forth about the branching of what arises from hypocrisy of blameworthy qualities, in His saying, ﴿And among people is one who says, "We believe in God and the Last Day"﴾ (Qur'an 2:8), in Surat al-Baqarah.

The sentence ﴿for each gate there is a designated portion of them﴾ is a description of *abwab* (gates). Its division by specific determination is known to God the Exalted. The pronoun in *minhum* refers to "those who follow you of the deviators," meaning: for each gate there is a group that enters through it, or for each level of the Fire there is a portion of the people of the Fire, apportioned according to the levels of the divisions of the Fire.

Know that these statements that came from Satan in the sacred presence are a disclosure of the innate nature of the development (*tatawwur*) through which the soul of Iblis took form from the time he refused to prostrate, and how each stage of that development emerged from what preceded it, until the satanic essence (*mahiyya*) was completed with its constituent elements, when he said, ﴿I will surely adorn [evil] for them on earth and will surely mislead them all, except Your sincere servants among them﴾ (Qur'an 15:39–40). Whenever a stage of that essence came into being in his nature, a statement came from him indicating it. This is like the testimony of the limbs speaking against the people of error on the Day of Reckoning.

As for the divine statements to which Satan's statements were answered, they manifest the commands of creation (*al-awamir al-takwiniyya*) which God decreed in His knowledge for the development of the stages of Iblis that constitute the reality of Satanhood (*shaytana*), and for the subtle favors which God has decreed for those of His servants who hold fast to them in resisting Satan's authority. Those statements are not all a debate between God and one of His creatures, nor a victory of Satan over his Creator, for his weakness before the might of his Creator does not reach to that.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 15, verses 45–48:

﴿Indeed, the God-fearing will be in gardens and springs.﴾ ﴿Enter them in peace, secure.﴾ ﴿And We will remove whatever resentment is in their breasts, as brothers, upon couches facing one another.﴾ ﴿No fatigue will touch them therein, nor will they be removed from it.﴾

This is a new sentence (isti'naf ibtida'i), a transition from the warning to the disbelievers to the good tidings for the God-fearing, following the Qur'an's habit of varying its style.

Al-muttaqun (the God-fearing): those characterized by taqwa (God-consciousness). This was discussed at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah.

Surah 55
Al-jannat (the gardens): the plural of jannah. It was discussed at His saying, Exalted is He, "that for them are gardens beneath which rivers flow," at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah.

Al-'uyun (the springs): the plural of 'ayn, which denotes an opening in the earth from which water emerges from the ground. Its gushing may occur without human effort, and its causes are many, as discussed at His saying, Exalted is He, "And among stones are those from which rivers gush forth," in Surat al-Baqarah. It may also occur through the action of an agent, which is tafjir (causing it to gush forth).

The clause "Enter them" (ud-khuluha) is governed by an omitted verb of speech, which is to be understood as a circumstantial clause (hal) describing the God-fearing, the indication being clear. The implied sense is: "It will be said to them, 'Enter them.'" The one who speaks is the angels, when the God-fearing enter the Garden. The ba' in bi-salam is for accompaniment (lil-musahabah).

Al-salam (peace): greeting. It was discussed at His saying, "And when those who believe in Our signs come to you, say: Peace be upon you," in Surat al-An'am.

Al-amn (security): deliverance from fear.

The clause "And We will remove whatever resentment is in their breasts" is coordinated (ma'tuf) upon the predicate, which is "in gardens and springs." The implied sense is: "Indeed, the God-fearing, We will remove whatever resentment is in their breasts."

Al-ghill, with a kasra on the ghayn, means hatred. It was discussed at His saying, Exalted is He, "And We will remove whatever resentment is in their breasts, beneath them rivers flow" [al-A'raf: 43], in Surat al-A'raf, meaning: whatever enmity existed among some of them in this world.

Ikhwanan (as brothers) is a circumstantial clause (hal), and it carries the sense of comparison, i.e., like brothers, meaning in the condition of brothers in this world.

The first to enter this generality are the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ, concerning the incidents that occurred among them, the impetus for which was difference of ijtihad (independent judgment) in establishing the interests of the Muslims, and severity in upholding the truth according to their respective ijtihad. As is narrated from 'Ali, may Allah honor his face, that he said: "I hope that I and Talhah will be among those of whom Allah, Exalted is He, said, 'And We will remove whatever resentment is in their breasts, as brothers.'" A foolish man from the Shi'ah of 'Ali, named (al-Harith ibn al-A'war al-Hamadani), said: "No, Allah is too just to gather you and Talhah in one place." 'Ali said: "Then to whom is this verse addressed? May your mother be bereaved, may dust be in your mouth!"

Al-Sururu (the couches): plural of sarir, a litter-like raised seat similar to a chair, spacious enough to recline upon. Al-ittika' (reclining) is the seat of those at ease and luxury, since one seated upon it can turn about as he wishes, and when he tires of one posture he turns to another.

Al-taqabul (facing one another): one being opposite another. It is included in the sense of companionship through sight and conversation.

Al-mass (touch): a metaphor for affliction.

Al-nasab (fatigue): the weariness arising from exertion of effort.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 15, verses 49–50:

﴿Inform My servants that I am the Forgiving, the Merciful.﴾ ﴿And that My punishment is the painful punishment.﴾ This is an introduction to the mention of the stories whose purpose in recalling them is admonition through what befell their people: the story of the people of Lot, the story of the companions of the Thicket (al-Aykah), and the story of Thamud.

This was begun with the story of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, because of what it contains of Allah's honour toward him, as an allusion to the polytheists, who did not follow his footsteps in monotheism.

So the sentence is a fresh resumption (istinaf ibtida'i), an independent opening, and it is connected to His saying at the beginning of the surah: ﴿And We did not destroy any town except that it had a known decree.﴾

The opening of the speech with the verb of informing (inba') is to arouse the eagerness of the listeners for what follows, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Has there reached you the news of the hosts?﴾ and similar. The intended matter is His saying, exalted is He, which comes later: ﴿And inform them about the guests of Ibrahim.﴾ He placed first the command to inform people of Allah's forgiveness and His punishment, beginning with the fundamental admonition before the admonition through the particulars of the events of retribution against the obstinate and the deliverance of those among them who were believers, because that revolves between the effect of forgiveness and the effect of punishment.
And forgiveness is mentioned before punishment because His mercy precedes His wrath.

The pronoun "anā" (I) and the pronoun "huwa" (He) are pronouns of separation (damir al-fasl), which serve to emphasise the predicate.

Know that in His saying, exalted is He, "Inform My servants ... the Merciful," there is among the embellishing figures of rhetoric (al-muhassinat al-badi'iyyah) the embellishment of balance (muhassin al-ittizan), when the yā' of "annī" is quiescent according to the reading of the majority, reciting it with its sukun, for the verse then comes measured according to the metre of the baḥr al-mujtatt, which has undergone al-khabn in its 'arud and its darb, so it is mutafʿilun fa'ilatun, twice.

[Page 58]

This conjunction (al-'atf), together with the fact that the verb being conjoined has the same form as the verb it is conjoined to, indicates that the intent is to report both matters. The reason for mentioning the story is that it is one of the manifestations of His mercy and His punishment, may He be exalted.

﴿And inform them about the guests of Abraham.﴾ ﴿When they entered upon him and said, "Peace," he said, "Indeed, we are fearful of you."﴾ ﴿They said, "Do not fear. Indeed, we give you good tidings of a knowledgeable boy."﴾ ﴿He said, "Do you give me good tidings although old age has touched me? Then about what do you give good tidings?"﴾ ﴿They said, "We have given you good tidings in truth, so do not be of those who despair."﴾ ﴿He said, "And who despairs of the mercy of his Lord except those who are astray?"﴾

"The guests of Abraham" (ḍayf Ibrāhīm) refers to the angels who had taken the form of strangers passing by his house. The story has already been mentioned in Surat Hud.

The clause "He said, 'Indeed, we are fearful of you'" (qāla innā minkum wajilūn) came without a conjunction (mafṣūlah), because it is an answer to the clause "they said, 'Peace'" (qālū salāman). His returning of the greeting has been omitted for brevity (ījāz), since it is evident, and it is stated explicitly in His saying, "He said, 'Peace, a people unknown'" (qāla salāmun qawmun munkarūn). That is, he said, "Indeed, we are fearful of you," after he had returned the greeting. In Surat Hud it is mentioned that he sensed fear from them when he saw that they did not extend their hands to eat.

The pronoun in "innā" (indeed, we) in Abraham's speech refers to himself and his household, because the guests had come to their house at a time when guests do not normally visit, so he thought they intended him harm. When they greeted him, he opened by asking for security, so he said, "Indeed, we are fearful of you," meaning, "You have frightened us." In Surat adh-Dhariyat it is mentioned that he said to them, "A people unknown."

Al-wajil means the fearful one, and al-wajal, with a fatḥah on the jīm, means fear. In Surat Hud the wording is "he did not recognize them and sensed fear from them" (nakirahum wa awjasa minhum khīfah).

In this verse the scattered parts of the angels' speech have been gathered together, and it has been limited to their reply to his statement, "Indeed, we are fearful of you." So the end of the answer is "Do not fear" (lā tawjal).

As for the clause "Indeed, we give you good tidings of a knowledgeable boy" (innā nubashshiruka bi-ghulāmin 'alīm), it is the resumption (isti'nāf) of another speech, after they had presented the hospitality to them, and his wife had been present, and they gave him good tidings in her presence, as explained in Surat Hud.

The "knowledgeable boy" (al-ghulām al-'alīm) is Isaac, peace be upon him, that is, one who is knowledgeable in the law (sharī'ah), by being a prophet.

Here their words to Abraham, peace be upon him, are reported, and in Surat Hud their words to his wife are reported. This is because the good tidings were for both of them together. It may be that they were received at one time, so they are two good tidings in terms of the one who receives them. It may also be that they occurred at two close times, in which they gave him the good tidings alone, then his wife came and they gave her the good tidings.

[Page 59]

Al-Jumhur (the majority of reciters) read "nubashshiruka" with a ḍammah on the nūn, a fatḥah on the bā', and a shaddah on the shīn with a kasrah, as the present tense of bashshara (with shaddah). Ḥamzah alone read "nabshuruka" with a fatḥah on the nūn, a sukūn on the bā', and a ḍammah on the shīn, and this is a dialectal form (lughah). It is said: basharahu yubashshiruhu, from the pattern naṣara.

The interrogative in "a-bashshartumūnī" (do you give me good tidings) is for wonder (li-t-ta'ajjub).

"'Alā" (upon/despite) here means "ma'a" (with), indicating the strong conjunction of the good tidings with old age touching him.

Al-massu means reaching or affliction. The meaning is: he wondered at their good tidings of a son, while old age had touched him.

This wonder is emphasized by the second interrogative in His saying, "Then about what do you give good tidings?" (fa-bi-ma tubashshirūn), which is an interrogative of wonder. The strange matter, which is known, has been treated as the unknown matter, because it is almost unknown.

Abraham, peace be upon him, knew from the good tidings that they were truthful angels, so it is determined that the interrogative is for wonder.

The object of "bashshartumūnī" is omitted because the context indicates it.

Nāfi' read "tubashshirūnī" with a kasrah on the nūn, lightened without ishbā' (lengthening), by omitting the nūn of the raf' (nominative ending) and omitting the yā' of the first person. All of this is a correct (faṣīḥ) form of lightening. Ibn Kathīr read it with a kasrah on the nūn, with shaddah, by omitting only the yā' of the first person. In Surat adh-Dhariyat it is mentioned that he said to them, "A people unknown."

Here their words to Abraham, peace be upon him, are reported, and in Surat Hud their words to his wife are reported. This is because the good tidings were for both of them together. It may be that they were received at one time, so they are two good tidings in terms of the one who receives them. It is said: basharahu yubashshiruhu, from the pattern naṣara.

The interrogative in "a-bashshartumūnī" (do you give me good tidings) is for wonder (li-t-ta'ajjub).

"'Alā" (upon/despite) here means "ma'a" (with), indicating the strong conjunction of the good tidings with old age touching him.

Al-massu means reaching or affliction. The meaning is: he wondered at their good tidings of a son, while old age had touched him.

This wonder is emphasized by the second interrogative in His saying, "Then about what do you give good tidings?" (fa-bi-ma tubashshirūn), which is an interrogative of wonder. The strange matter, which is known, has been treated as the unknown matter, because it is almost unknown.

Nāfi' read "tubashshirūnī" with a kasrah on the nūn, lightened without ishbā' (lengthening), by omitting the nūn of the raf' (nominative ending) and omitting the yā' of the first person. So their words are a response to his words, not an answer to his interrogative, because it was not a genuine interrogative.

Then they forbade him from considering it unlikely, saying that it is to consider the mercy of the All-Powerful unlikely. After he knew that those who gave the good tidings were sent to him from God, considering it unlikely leads to despair

[Page 60]

of God's mercy. So they said, "Do not be of those who despair" (fa-lā takun mina l-qānṭīn). That is because, when he considered it unlikely, in the manner of one who wonders at its occurrence, this was a trace of the deep rootedness of ordinary matters in his soul, so that the news whose truth he knew did not uproot them from him. A remnant of hesitation about its occurrence remained in his soul, so his state came close to the state of those who despair of God's command. Since Abraham, peace be upon him, was free from despair of God's mercy, they addressed his admonition in the appropriate manner of courtesy, forbidding him from being among the company of those who despair. This was a warning to him against what would place him in that company, and they did not assume that he himself was despairing, because of the elevated rank of his prophethood above that. In this situation he was like his situation in the context that God relates from him: "Show me how You give life to the dead. He said, 'Have you not believed?' When the angels alerted him with the slightest alert, he was reminded.

﴿He said, "What then is your business, O messengers?"﴾ ﴿They said, "We have been sent to a guilty people,﴾ ﴿except the family of Lot. Indeed, we will save them all,﴾ ﴿except his wife. We have decreed that she will be among those who remain behind."﴾

This dialogue between Abraham and the angels (peace be upon them) is related because it combines two things: showing the virtue of Abraham (peace be upon him) and warning the Quraysh by what befell some of the nations that denied their messengers. Abraham (peace be upon him) moved on to ask them about the reason for their descent to the earth, because he knew that the angels do not descend except for a great matter, as God, the Exalted, said: ﴿We do not send down the angels except with truth﴾ (15:8). The angels were sent down on the Day of Badr to annihilate the chiefs and leaders of the polytheists.

The word *khatb* (affair, business) has already occurred in God's words ﴿He said, "What is your business, O women?"﴾ in Surat Yusuf.

The "guilty people" are the people of Sodom and its towns, and their mention has already occurred in Surat Hud.

The exception in ﴿except the family of Lot﴾ is *munqati'* (disconnected exception, i.e., not of the same category as what precedes), because they were not guilty. The exception in ﴿except his wife﴾ is *muttasil* (connected exception, i.e., of the same category), because she was from the family of Lot.

The clause ﴿Indeed, we will save them all﴾ is a *isti'naf bayani* (explanatory resumptive clause), explaining the generality contained in the exception of the family of Lot from the object of the verb *arsalna* (we have sent), in order to repel the possibility that they had not been sent to them or commanded to save them.

In the phrase ﴿We have been sent to a guilty people﴾ there is *ijaz hadhf* (conciseness through omission). The complete sense is: "We have been sent to Lot, for the sake of a guilty people," that is, to punish them. This implies the exception in ﴿except the family of Lot﴾.

[Page 62]

The majority of reciters read *lamunajjuhum* with a fathah on the nun and a shaddah on the jim, as the imperfect of *najja* (doubled form). Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read it with a kasrah on the nun and without a shaddah on the jim, as the imperfect of *anja* (hamzated form).

The attribution of the decree (*taqdir*) to the pronoun of the angels is because they are resolved on its cause, which is what they were entrusted with: warning Lot (peace be upon him) and his family against looking back at the punishment, and their leaving off warning his wife, until she looked back and there befell her what befell the people of Lot.

The majority of reciters read *qaddarna* with a shaddah on the dal, from *al-taqdir* (decreeing). Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, read it with no shaddah on the dal, from *qadara* (the unaugmented form). Both are dialects.

The clause ﴿Indeed, she is among those who remain behind﴾ is resumptive (*mustani'afah*), and *inna* here is a *mu'allaqah* (suspending particle) for the verb *qaddarna*, preventing it from governing its object. The original sense of the statement is *ghuburuha*, that is, her departure and her destruction.

Suspension (*ta'liq*) may affect all verbs, but it occurs most frequently with verbs of the heart and is rarer with others, and it is not, in verification, one of their specific features.

The mention of *al-ghabirin* (those who remain behind) has already occurred in Surat al-A'raf.

The exception in ﴿except his wife﴾ is *muttasil* (connected exception, i.e., of the same category), because she was from the family of Lot.

The clause ﴿Indeed, we will save them all﴾ is a *isti'naf bayani* (explanatory resumptive clause), explaining the generality contained in the exception of the family of Lot from the object of the verb *arsalna* (we have sent), in order to repel the possibility that they had not been sent to them or commanded to save them.

In the phrase ﴿We have been sent to a guilty people﴾ there is *ijaz hadhf* (conciseness through omission). The complete sense is: "We have been sent to Lot, for the sake of a guilty people," that is, to punish them. This implies the exception in ﴿except the family of Lot﴾.

[Page 62]

The majority of reciters read *lamunajjuhum* with a fathah on the nun and a shaddah on the jim, as the imperfect of *najja* (doubled form). Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read it with a kasrah on the nun and without a shaddah on the jim, as the imperfect of *anja* (hamzated form).

The attribution of the decree (*taqdir*) to the pronoun of the angels is because they are resolved on its cause, which is what they were entrusted with: warning Lot (peace be upon him) and his family against looking back at the punishment, and their leaving off warning his wife, until she looked back and there befell her what befell the people of Lot.

The majority of reciters read *qaddarna* with a shaddah on the dal, from *al-taqdir* (decreeing). Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, read it with no shaddah on the dal, from *qadara* (the unaugmented form). Both are dialects.

The clause ﴿Indeed, she is among those who remain behind﴾ is resumptive (*mustani'afah*), and *inna* here is a *mu'allaqah* (suspending particle) for the verb *qaddarna*, preventing it from governing its object. The original sense of the statement is *ghuburuha*, that is, her departure and her destruction.

Suspension (*ta'liq*) may affect all verbs, but it occurs most frequently with verbs of the heart and is rarer with others, and it is not, in verification, one of their specific features.

The mention of *al-ghabirin* (those who remain behind) has already occurred in Surat al-A'raf.

[Page 63]

A continuation (*tafri'*) on the account of their story with Abraham. What is known about the angels leaving Abraham has been omitted. The implied sense is: they parted from him, went to Lot, and "when they came to Lot."

This is a rejection (*idrab*) of his statement "Indeed you are a people unknown," and a negation of his assumption that they were ordinary humans whose tribe he did not know, so he could not be sure they would not harm him.

We should therefore explain the features of this Arabic structure.

The repetition of the verb *ataynaka* (أتَيْناكَ) after the conjunction *wa* (وَ), although *ataynaka* is synonymous with *jinnaka* (جِئْناكَ), rather than saying *wa-bil-haqq* alone, may be for lexical emphasis through a synonym. The use of the root *ma-ja-a* (مجيء) in one verb and *a-ta-a* (إتيان) in the other may be merely for stylistic variety, to avoid repeating the same verb, like His saying in Surat al-Furqan: ﴿And they bring you no example but that We bring you the truth and better explanation﴾. On this reading, the *ba'* (بِ) in *bima kanu fihi yamtarun* and in *bil-haqq* expresses association (*mula-basah*).

[Page 64]

It is also possible that the *ba'* in the second verb, *wa-atayناka*, has a specific function that the conjunction *wa* cannot fulfil: the attention to the difference between the two prepositional objects, each fitting the verb it is attached to. Since what is attached to *jinnaka* is a sensory matter, namely the punishment they used to doubt, and what can be attributed to the verb *maji'* (مجيء) in a quasi-literal sense, being a well-known figurative coming equal to the literal, the verb *jinnaka* was chosen so that it is attributed to the pronoun of the addressees, and what they used to doubt is attached to it. The *ba'* attached to it is for transitivity, because they "brought" the punishment. His saying *bima kanu fihi yamtarun* is in the position of a direct object, as when you say *dhahabtu bihi* (ذَهَبْتُ بِهِ, "I took him away") meaning *adhhabtuhu* (أذْهَبْتُهُ, "I made him go"), even if you did not go with him. Do you not see His saying: ﴿Then whether We take you away﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 41], meaning "We remove you from the world," i.e., "We cause you to die"? This *ba'* is for transitivity and functions as the transitive *hamzah*.

As for the object of the verb *atayناka*, which is *bil-haqq* (بِالحَقِّ), it is an abstract matter that cannot itself be the thing "brought." So the verb *atayna* does not take the verb of coming as its object. The root of *maji'* was therefore changed to the root of *ita'* (إتيان), as a signal that a meaning other than that of the previous verb is intended, namely the figurative coming. This *ita'* is attributed to the angels in its literal meaning, and in their coming they were associated with the truth, i.e., the truthfulness. Truthfulness is not something to which the coming is attributed. So the *ba'* in His saying *bil-haqq* expresses association, not transitivity.

*Al-qit'* (القِطْع), with a kasra on the *qaf* and a sukun on the *ta'*, is the last part of the night. It was mentioned earlier at His saying ﴿as if their faces were covered with pieces of the dark night﴾ in Surat Yunus.

They commanded him to put his family in front of him, while he himself would be behind them. So he follows *adbarahum* (أدْبارَهم, "their backs"), that is, their rear, so that he would be like a shield between them and the punishment that would descend on his people immediately after their departure, as an honour to the Messenger, peace be upon him. Also, they commanded him that none of his family should turn back toward the dwellings of their people, because the punishment would have already descended upon their dwellings. Since he was behind his family, they feared turning back, because he would be watching them. The details of this have been explained in Surat Hud, and that his wife turned back and the punishment befell her.

[Page 65]

*Wa-haythu tu'marun* (وَحَيْثُ تُؤْمَرُونَ), i.e., "wherever you are commanded," meaning wherever you are commanded to proceed. They did not tell him the place they were heading to until the time of departure. It is the city of *Amurriyah* (عَمُّورِيَّة), as was mentioned earlier in Surat Hud.

On this reading, the *ba'* (بِ) in *bima kanu fihi yamtarun* and in *bil-haqq* expresses association (*mula-basah*).

[Page 64]

It is also possible that the *ba'* in the second verb, *wa-atayناka*, has a specific function that the conjunction *wa* cannot fulfil: the attention to the difference between the two prepositional objects, each fitting the verb it is attached to. Since what is attached to *jinnaka* is a sensory matter, namely the punishment they used to doubt, and what can be attributed to the verb *maji'* (مجيء) in a quasi-literal sense, being a well-known figurative coming equal to the literal, the verb *jinnaka* was chosen so that it is attributed to the pronoun of the addressees, and what they used to doubt is attached to it. The *ba'* attached to it is for transitivity, because they "brought" the punishment. His saying *bima kanu fihi yamtarun* is in the position of a direct object, as when you say *dhahabtu bihi* (ذَهَبْتُ بِهِ, "I took him away") meaning *adhhabtuhu* (أذْهَبْتُهُ, "I made him go"), even if you did not go with him. Do you not see His saying: ﴿Then whether We take you away﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 41], meaning "We remove you from the world," i.e., "We cause you to die"? This *ba'* is for transitivity and functions as the transitive *hamzah*.

As for the object of the verb *atayناka*, which is *bil-haqq* (بِالحَقِّ), it is an abstract matter that cannot itself be the thing "brought." So the verb *atayna* does not take the verb of coming as its object. The root of *maji'* was therefore changed to the root of *ita'* (إتيان), as a signal that a meaning other than that of the previous verb is intended, namely the figurative coming. This *ita'* is attributed to the angels in its literal meaning, and in their coming they were associated with the truth, i.e., the truthfulness. Truthfulness is not something to which the coming is attributed. So the *ba'* in His saying *bil-haqq* expresses association, not transitivity.

*Al-qit'* (القِطْع), with a kasra on the *qaf* and a sukun on the *ta'*, is the last part of the night. It was mentioned earlier at His saying ﴿as if their faces were covered with pieces of the dark night﴾ in Surat Yunus.

They commanded him to put his family in front of him, while he himself would be behind them. So he follows *adbarahum* (أدْبارَهم, "their backs"), that is, their rear, so that he would be like a shield between them and the punishment that would descend on his people immediately after their departure, as an honour to the Messenger, peace be upon him. Also, they commanded him that none of his family should turn back toward the dwellings of their people, because the punishment would have already descended upon their dwellings. Since he was behind his family, they feared turning back, because he would be watching them. The details of this have been explained in Surat Hud, and that his wife turned back and the punishment befell her.

[Page 65]

*Wa-haythu tu'marun* (وَحَيْثُ تُؤْمَرُونَ), i.e., "wherever you are commanded," meaning wherever you are commanded to proceed. They did not tell him the place they were heading to until the time of departure. It is the city of *Amurriyah* (عَمُّورِيَّة), as was mentioned earlier in Surat Hud.

He and the (inserted) meaning: **qaḍaynā** (We decreed) means *qaddarnā* (We determined). The verb was used with the implicit sense of *awḥaynā* (We revealed), so it takes **ilā** (to). The sense is: "We decreed that matter and revealed to him," that is, to Lut, peace be upon him, revealing to him what We had decreed.

**Dhālika al-amr** (that matter) is an indefinite reference used for awe, and the demonstrative is used for magnification, meaning "that great matter."

The clause **anna dābira hā'ulā'i maqṭūʿun** ("that the last of these people is cut off") explains **dhālika al-amr**. It is suited to the implicit verb *awḥaynā*. The sense becomes: "We decreed the matter and revealed to him that the last of these people is cut off." The speech is thus arranged in this wondrous and rich-meaning form, with the vagueness and magnification contained in the phrase **dhālika al-amr**.

The coming of the clause **dābir** as an explanation, together with the suitability of **anna** for clarifying both the vagueness of the demonstrative and the implicit, tadmin-based verb **awḥaynā** (the device of tadmin, implying one verb in the sense of another), achieves a wondrous brevity (ījāz) of miraculous character.

**Al-dābir** means the last, that is, the last person.

**Qaṭʿuhu** means its removal, and it is a kināya (metonymy) for their complete annihilation, as was mentioned earlier at His words, ﴿So the last of the people who did wrong was cut off﴾ [al-An'am: 45] in Surat al-An'am.

The demonstrative **hā'ulā'** refers to his people.

**Muṣbiḥīn** means entering into the morning, that is, at its beginning. It is a ḥāl (circumstantial state) of the demonstrative noun. The beginning of the morning is the time of sunrise, and for this reason He said after it, ﴿So the Cry seized them at sunrise﴾ [al-Ḥijr: 73].

Page 66

﴿And the people of the city came, rejoicing.﴾ ﴿He said, "These are my guests, so do not disgrace me.﴾ ﴿And fear God and do not humiliate me."﴾ This is a conjunctive continuation (*ʿaṭf*, coordination) of a part of the story of the people of Lot, and it is the most important part of it.

The arrival of the people of the city to him, and their discussion with him, took place before he knew that they were angels. Had he known that, he would not have feared what the people of the city had resolved upon. He learned what they had resolved only after their argument with him, as in God's words, ﴿They said, "O Lot, we are messengers of your Lord; they shall not reach you"﴾ [Hud: 81], in the Surah of Hud. The conjunctive particle *wāw* (and) does not indicate that what follows it is sequential.

It is permissible to take the clause as being in the position of a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) either from the concealed pronoun (*ḍamīr mustatir*) of Lot in the verb *qāla* in ﴿He said, "Indeed you are a people unknown"﴾ [al-Hijr: 62], or from the *hāʾ* in *ilayhi* (to him). In that case there is no difficulty. The city is Sodom. *Yastabshirūn* means they rejoice and are delighted. It is the reflexive/intransitive form (*muṭāwaʿ*) of *bashsharahu*, "he gave him good news," so that *istabshara* means "he became glad." God says, ﴿Then rejoice in your bargain﴾ [al-Tawbah: 111], in the Surah of Bara'ah. It is expressed in the imperfect form (*muḍāriʿ*) to indicate renewal and recurrence, as an intensification of their joy. That is because they had learned that strange men had lodged in the house of Lot, peace be upon him, so they rejoiced at this in order to sodomize them, in keeping with their evil habit. The story has already been discussed in the Surah of Hud.

*Al-fazḥ* and *al-faḍīḥah* mean the spread of a shameful state. They used to take pride in mistreating the guest, and this was regarded as a humiliation for his host. He reminded them of the religious restraint, even though they were disbelievers, in pursuit of the thoroughness of the call with which he had come, and of the customary restraint (*wāziʿ ʿurfī*), so he said, ﴿And fear God and do not humiliate me,﴾ as in the words of ʿAbd Banī al-Ḥiḥāsh:

*Gray hair and Islam suffice a man as a restrainer.*

*Al-khizy* means abasement and humiliation. It was discussed in God's words, ﴿except for disgrace in the life of this world﴾ [al-Baqarah: 85], at the beginning of the Surah of al-Baqarah, and it was discussed in a similar story in the Surah of Hud.
