﴿They said: Did we not forbid you from (dealing with) the people?﴾ ﴿He said: These are my daughters, if you are going to act.﴾ ﴿By your life, they were wandering blindly in their intoxication.﴾ ﴿So the Cry seized them at sunrise.﴾ ﴿We turned it upside down and rained down upon them stones of baked clay.﴾ ﴿Indeed in that are signs for those who discern.﴾ ﴿And it is on a road that remains.﴾ ﴿Indeed in that is a sign for the believers.﴾

The "wa" (and) in "Did we not forbid you" is a conjunction (*'atf*) upon the speech of Lot, peace be upon him, following the manner of conjoining upon the speech of another, as in His saying ﴿He said: And from my descendants﴾ (al-Baqarah: 124), after His saying ﴿He said: I am making you a leader for mankind﴾ (al-Baqarah: 124) in Surat al-Baqarah.

The interrogation is one of denial (*istifham inkari*), and what is conjoined is the denial.

"Al-'alamin" means the people. The prohibition is extended to the persons of "al-'alamin" by way of an omitted modifier (*taqdir mudaf*) indicated by the context, meaning: Did we not forbid you from protecting the people or from granting them protection (*ijara*)? That is, it was incumbent upon you to leave us between ourselves and our custom, so that travellers would not hope to be protected by you. They used to cut the road, attacking those who passed by their settlements. "Al-'alamin" was already mentioned in al-Fatihah, and they intended by it here the categories of tribes, for the purpose of generalisation.

He offered them his daughters, thinking that this would deter them and quench their lust, and for this reason he said ﴿if you are going to act﴾.

The meaning of his offering his daughters was explained in Surat Hud, and the phrase "my daughters" may refer to his own daughters, who were two or three, and it may refer to the daughters of all the people, treating them as his daughters, since the Prophet is like a father to his community.

The sentence ﴿By your life, they were wandering blindly in their intoxication﴾ is a parenthetical insertion (*i'tiraD*) between the parts of the story, as a lesson on the futility of admonition for one who is in the intoxication of his desire.

[Page 68]

Its addressee is Muhammad ﷺ from God, the Exalted. It has also been said that it is from the speech of the angels, with an implied "saying" (*qawl*).

The word "la'amrika" is a form of oath, and the lam that enters upon the word "'amr" is the lam of oath.

"Al-'amr," with a fatha on the 'ayn and a sukun on the mim, is originally a dialect form of "al-'umr" with a damma on the 'ayn. The fatha form was specialised for the formula of oath because of its lightness, since the oath occurs frequently in speech. It is an oath by the life of the one addressed. In usage, when the lam of oath enters upon it, they put it in the nominative as a subject (*mubtada'*) with an obligatorily omitted predicate (*khabar*), and the estimate is: ﴿By your life, my oath is﴾.

This is one of the places where the predicate is omitted by obligatory deletion in Arab usage, being sufficed by the indication of the lam for the meaning of oath. They may also use it without the lam, and in that case they join it to the name of God and put both in the accusative, as in the saying of 'Umar ibn Abi Rabi'a:

*"By your life, Allah, how can the two meet?"*

Here "'amr" is put in the accusative by removing the preposition, which is the ba' of oath, and the name of God is put in the accusative as the object of the verbal noun, meaning: by your "ta'mir" of God, that is, by your glorifying God, that is, your saying "by God, by your life," as glorification of God; since swearing by the name of anyone is glorification of him. Thus the expression of oath is used as a metaphor (*kinaya*) for glorification, just as the expression of greeting is used as a metaphor for glorification in the words of the tashahhud, "The greetings are for God." That is, "I swear to you by your glorification of your Lord." This is what appears to me as the explanation of the accusative, although I have differed here somewhat from the statements of the lexicographers, in order to remove the difficulty that they encountered.

"Al-sakra" is the loss of reason. It is derived from "al-sakr," with a fatha on the sin, which means blocking and closing. It is applied here to error, as a comparison: the overwhelming of the impulses of desire over the impulses of right guidance is likened to the loss and covering of reason.

"Ya'mahun" means they are bewildered and do not find guidance. It was already discussed at His saying ﴿He extends for them in their transgression, they wander blindly﴾ (al-Baqarah: 15) in Surat al-Baqarah.

[Page 69]

The sentence ﴿So the Cry seized them at sunrise﴾ is a consequence (*tafri'*) upon the sentence ﴿And We decreed that matter for him﴾ (al-Hijr: 66).

"Al-sayha" is a thunderbolt in the air. It consists of thunderbolts and earthquakes, and in it are stones of baked clay, whose explanation has already passed in Surat Hud.

"Mushriqin" is put in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*hal*) from the pronoun of absence. It is an active participle from "ashraqu," meaning they entered the time of sunrise.

The two pronouns in ﴿its upper part its lower part﴾ refer to the city. The pronoun in "'alayhim" refers to what the plural pronouns before it referred to.

The sentence ﴿Indeed in that are signs for those who discern﴾ is a concluding tailpiece (*tadhyil*).

"Al-ayat" are proofs, that is, indications of realities of guidance and its opposite, and of the exposure of the deniers to their messengers to a severe punishment.

The demonstrative "dhalika" refers to all that the story beginning with His saying ﴿And inform them about the guests of Abraham﴾ (al-Hijr: 51) contained. In it are signs: the sign of the descent of the angels into the house of Abraham, peace be upon him, as an honour to him; the good news to him of a knowing son; God's informing him of what would befall the people of Lot, as an honour to Abraham, peace be upon them both; God's support of Lot through the angels; the rescue of Lot, peace be upon him, and his family; the destruction of his people and his wife, for her support of them; the sign of the blindness of the people of error to the proofs of repentance; and the sign of God's anger at those who persist in disobeying the messengers.

The discussion of the word "aya" was already given at His saying ﴿And those who disbelieved and denied Our signs﴾ (al-Baqarah: 39) in Surat al-Baqarah, and at His saying ﴿They say: Why has no sign been sent down to him from his Lord?﴾ (al-An'am: 37) in Surat al-An'am.

"Al-mutawassimun" are those possessing *tawassum*, which is reflection upon the mark (*sima*), that is, the sign indicating the landmark. What is meant is those who reflect on causes and their consequences, and these are the believers. This is an allusion (*ta'ridh*) against those whom admonitions did not deter, that they are below the rank of reflection, an allusion to the polytheists

[Page 70]

who did not take heed, that there would befall them what befell the nations before them, whose reports they knew and whose traces they saw.

For this reason He followed the sentence with the sentence ﴿And it is on a road that remains﴾, that is, the city mentioned just now is on an enduring road, many of you witness its traces in the land of Palestine, on the road of your trade to Syria and its surroundings. This is like His saying ﴿And indeed you pass by them in the morning﴾ (al-Saffat: 137) ﴿and at night. Will you not understand?﴾ (al-Saffat: 138).

"Al-muqim" originally means the person who is settled in his place, not departing. Here it is borrowed for the remaining traces of the city in its place, by likening them to a settled person.

The sentence ﴿Indeed in that is a sign for the believers﴾ is a tailpiece (*tadhyil*). The demonstrative refers to what was mentioned before of the story, together with what was added to it of reminder that their settlements clearly bear the traces of the sinking and of the rain of heated stones. He expressed it in the tailpiece with "the believers" to draw attention to the fact that those who reflect are the believers.

He made that "a sign" in the singular as a variation of style (*tafannun*), because "aya" is a collective noun that applies to the plural. Moreover, the totality of what befell them is one sign with respect to the purpose of the story, which is the end of the deniers. Within the folds of those signs are signs. As for the difference between the plural "signs" at the beginning and the singular here, what is recounted of the story of Lot and the guests of Abraham, and of what their final affair was, each part of that is in itself a sign, so the demonstrative refers to a number of signs. As for the fact that the town of Lot is "on an enduring road," this in its totality is one sign. So consider this.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 15, verse 78:

﴿And indeed, the companions of the thicket were wrongdoers.﴾ ﴿So We took retribution from them.﴾ [al-Hijr: 79]

He joined one narrative to another because of the admonition found in both of them. The mention of these two joined narratives is a complement and an incidental insertion (idmaj), since there is no connection between them and what precedes them of the story of Ibrahim

Page 71

and the angels. He singled out for mention the companions of the thicket (Ashab al-Aykah) and the companions of al-Hijr, because they are like the people of Lut in admonishing the polytheists among the angels; for the people of Makkah witness the dwellings of these three nations.

"In" (إنْ) is the light (mukhaffafah) form of "inna," and its governing function has been nullified by the lightening, so it entered upon a verbal sentence. The lam that enters upon "la-zalimin" is the lam of distinction (al-lam al-fariqah) between "inna," whose original form is doubled, and the negating "in."

Al-Aykah: the thicket, a dense growth of trees intertwined with one another. Its collective noun is "ayk." Here it is used with the intended sense of a category (al-jins), since their dwellings were in a thicket of many trees and foliage. The word may also be lightened, so it is said "laykah."

The companions of the thicket are the people of Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, and they are the people of Madyan. It has been said that the companions of the thicket are a group of Shu'ayb's people other than the people of Madyan: the people of Madyan were the town dwellers, and the companions of the thicket were their desert-dwelling folk. Shu'ayb was a messenger to all of them. God, exalted is He, said (﴿The companions of the thicket denied the messengers﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 176] ﴿When Shu'ayb said to them, "Will you not be mindful of God?"﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 177]), and the discussion of this will come in full in the surah of al-Shu'ara.

Al-zalimun: the polytheists.

Al-intiqam: punishment for a sin, derived from al-naqm, which is disapproval of an act. It is said "naqama 'alayhi," as in this verse, and also "naqama minhu." It was mentioned earlier in His saying (﴿And you hold nothing against us except﴾ [al-A'raf: 126]) in surah al-A'raf. The retribution is stated in general terms in this verse and is explained in other verses, such as the verse in surah Hud.

The pronoun in (innahuma) refers to the town of Lot's people and the Thicket (al-Aykah), the people of Shu'ayb, peace be upon them both.

Al-Imam: the clear road, because the traveller follows it (ya'tammu bihi al-sa'ir), meaning he knows that it leads [to his destination], since nothing of it is hidden from him. Al-Mubin: the evident, the plain. That is, both towns lie along the route of the caravans, which passes by the people of Makkah.

Allah's statement earlier, ﴿And indeed it is on a road that remains﴾ [al-Hijr: 76], has already preceded. So the inclusion of the town of Lot, peace be upon him, in the pronoun here is an emphasis on the first mention.

It appears that the dual pronoun refers to the companions of the Thicket, considering that they were two tribes: Madyan, and the original inhabitants of the thicket among whom Madyan settled. Ibrahim, peace be upon him, settled his son Madyan in the east of the land of al-Khalil, and [a settlement] can only exist in an inhabited land. In my view, this is what is implied by the mention of the people of Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, by the name Madyan on several occasions and by the name the companions of the Thicket on other occasions. More explanation of this will come in Surah al-Shu'ara'.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 15, verses 80–84:**

﴿And the companions of al-Hijr did deny the messengers.﴾ ﴿And We gave them Our signs, but they were turning away from them.﴾ ﴿And they used to carve houses out of the mountains, feeling secure.﴾ ﴿So the Blast seized them at morning.﴾ ﴿So what they used to earn did not avail them.﴾

The stories of these three nations were gathered in one sequence: the people of Lut, the companions of al-Aykah, and the companions of al-Hijr, because of the similarity of the punishment that was inflicted on them, which was the punishment of the Blast (al-Sayhah), the Quake (al-Rajfah), and the Thunderbolt (al-Sa'iqah).

The companions of al-Hijr are Thamud, who used to dwell in al-Hijr, pronounced with a kasra on the ha' and a sukun on the jim. Al-Hijr means a restricted place, that is, a place prohibited to people because of its being specially set apart for someone, or it is derived from ḥijārah (stone), because they carved their houses in the rock of the mountain with firm carving. Layers were made in it, and in its middle there was a great well and many wells.

Al-Hijr is the place known as Wadi al-Qura, which lies between Medina and Syria, and which is known today by the name Madain Salih, on the road from Khaybar to Tabuk.

As for Hajr al-Yamamah, the city of Banu Hanifah, it is pronounced with a fatha on the ha'. It is in the land of Najd and is called al-'Urud, and today it is part of the land of Bahrain.

Some Orientalists from among the Europeans have imagined that the houses carved in that mountain were tombs, and they clung to fanciful arguments. Among what refutes their claims is the emptiness of those caves of human bodies. And if those were tombs, where were the dwellings of the living?

The apparent meaning is that when the Blast seized Thamud, they were scattered outside the houses, because of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So the Blast seized them at morning﴾. Small niches have been found at the entrances of those houses, which indicate that they were made for closing the doors of the entrances at night.

The definite article in "the messengers" (al-mursalin) is generic (li-l-jins), so it applies to one messenger, since the meaning is that they denied Salih, peace be upon him. This is like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿The people of Noah denied the messengers﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 105], which has already been mentioned. Likewise, the plural of "signs" in His saying "Our signs" (ayatina) is intended generically. It refers to the sign of the she-camel, or it is meant that it was one sign that comprised several signs in the manner of its emergence from a rock, its life, its grazing, and its drinking. It has been narrated that her young camel went out with her, so they were two signs.

The clause ﴿and they used to carve﴾ is a parenthetical clause (mu'taridah, an interposed clause), and naht means cutting a stone or wood from its middle or from its sides.

"From the mountains" (min al-jibal) is a partitive (tab'id) connected to "they carve" (yanhituna). The meaning is "from the rock of the mountains," due to what the verb "they carve" indicates.

"Feeling secure" (aminin) is a circumstantial clause (hal) of the pronoun in "they carve," and it is a anticipated circumstance (hal muqaddarah), meaning they were intending to be secure after carving them and dwelling in them. They were for them like fortresses, where the enemy could not reach them.

But they forgot that these could not secure them from the punishment of God. Therefore He said, ﴿So what they used to earn did not avail them﴾.

The fa' in ﴿So the Blast seized them﴾ indicates sequence and causation, and "at morning" (musbihin) is a circumstantial clause, meaning they entered the time of morning.

﴿What they used to earn﴾ means what they used to make, that is, the houses which they took care to fortify and beautify, as the verb "used to" (kanu) indicates. The form of the present tense in "they earn" (yaksibun) is for its indication of repetition and renewal, which is a metonymy for perfecting the craft. For this reason, the placement of the relative pronoun and its clause is more eloquent than the placement of a word such as "their houses," to indicate that what did not avail them anything is something that was made for availing, and it is characteristic of it to do so.

Page 75

The placement of the waw at the beginning of this sentence is remarkable. This sentence is suitable to serve as a concluding generalization (tadhyil) to the accounts of the punished nations, showing that what befell them was deserved. It is part of God's justice in recompensing deeds according to what suits them. It is also suitable to serve as an introduction to the sentence that follows it, namely ﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming﴾. The intended meaning is the Hour of the recompense of those who denied Muhammad (ﷺ), that is, the Hour of Resurrection. On the first reading the waw is parenthetical (i'tiradiyya) or circumstantial (haliyya). On the second reading it is conjunctive ( 'atifa), joining one sentence to another and one predicate to another.

Page 75 (continued)

However, the conjunction may occur in both cases so that the sentence stands independently in conveying its content, because of its importance, even though it also completes what precedes it. What gave this sentence this remarkable position is the inimitable arrangement of the sentences (nazm al-jumal al-mu'jiz) and the movement from one purpose to another through the relevance that links them.

"The heavens and the earth and what is between them" includes all kinds of created beings, animals and inanimate things. It includes the nations that are on the earth and what befell them. It includes the angels charged with sending down punishment. It includes the cosmic events that struck the nations, such as earthquakes, thunderbolts and falling fragments.

The bi' in ﴿except with truth﴾ is of association (lil-mulabasa) and is connected to ﴿We created﴾. The meaning is: a creation associated with truth and accompanied by it, such that truth is manifest in all the conditions of created beings.

The association here is customary ('urfiyya). The manifestation of truth may be delayed relative to the creation of some conditions and events, with varying delay. Thus the association between creation and truth varies according to the states of the manifestation and concealment of truth. Yet truth does not remain hidden for long; it appears in the final outcome of affairs, as indicated by the saying of God, the Exalted: ﴿Rather, We hurl the truth against falsehood, and it crushes it, and behold, it vanishes﴾ (al-Anbiya', 21:18).

Truth here is the ordering of the conditions of created beings according to a system suited to wisdom and fitness, in good and evil, perfection and deficiency, elevation and abasement, in every kind, according to what befits its quiddity and reality and what sets it right and what it is fit for, in accordance with what the general order requires and not according to desires and appetites. When that described truth is evident, its existence accompanying the existence of what it is due to, the matter is clear. When the deviation of something from a fitting order appears, then through reflection and inquiry it becomes clear that behind that lies a fitness that required the suspension of the due accompaniment. Then truth is not changed in the end.

This interpretation is shown by the placement of the verse after the mention of the punishment of the nations that rebelled and oppressed. That punishment is a fitting recompense for their rebellion and corruption. Even though they were granted respite for a time, by a mercy from God and for the wisdom of preserving the habitation of part of the world for a period, they did not escape the punishment they deserved. That too is part of truth. Their respite was only truth, and the descent of punishment upon them was only truth when its causes arrived, namely their rebellion against their prophets. The same applies to the recompense of the Hereafter: it may be suspended in this world because of the suspension of what the general or particular wisdom required.

Page 76

The position of the sentence ﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming﴾ in the discourse makes it like the conclusion of an argument. Whoever knows that all created beings were created in a manner associated with truth, and is certain of this, knows that truth does not fail to reach its due, even if it is absent and delayed. Although the order of worldly events may suspend the manifestation of truth in its proper place and its failure to reach its owners, he knows that behind this order there is a reserved order in which truth connects with every deserving one, whether for good or for evil. So let no one who escaped those who did wrong before the punishment befell them think that he has escaped recompense. God has prepared another world in which He gives affairs to their deserving ones.

Therefore God followed ﴿We did not create the heavens and the earth﴾ with the verse ﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming﴾. That is, the hour in which truth is enforced is certainly coming, so do not be disturbed by what you see of the safety and respite of those who deny you, as God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And whether We show you some of what We threaten them with, or We take you in death, to Us is their return; then God is witness over what they do﴾ (Yunus, 10:46). The purpose of this is to console the Prophet (ﷺ) for the harm he suffered from the polytheists, their denial, and their persistence in it until a known term.

This sentence, by the measure of the outward meaning, deserved to be separated without a conjunction, because its proper form is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf). But it was conjoined, to present it in the form of an independent statement, out of concern for its content, and because it consoles the Messenger (ﷺ) for what he meets from his people. It also allows the command to pardon them in this world to be grammatically consequent upon it, because their recompense is left to the appointed time.

In God's giving respite to the polytheists and then saving them from the punishment of extermination, there is a wisdom by which God's purpose is realized: the continuation of this religion and its spread in the world through the Arabs conveying it and carrying it to the nations.

Page 77

The Hour here means the Hour of Resurrection, which is the subject with which the sūra opens. This is a shift from threatening them with worldly punishment to threatening them with the punishment of the Hereafter. A similar meaning is found in the saying of God, the Exalted: ﴿We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them except with truth and for a specified term; but those who disbelieve turn away from what they are warned of﴾ (al-Ahqaf, 46:3), in the sūra of al-Ahqaf.

The consequence ﴿So forgive with gracious forgiveness﴾ following the saying of God, the Exalted, ﴿We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them except with truth﴾ is in terms of its implied meaning (kinaya). That meaning is that the recompense for their deeds is left to God, the Exalted. For this reason He commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to turn away from their harm and their poor reception of the call.

Al-safh means pardon, and it has been mentioned before in the saying of God, the Exalted: ﴿So pardon them and overlook﴾ (al-Ma'ida, 5:13), in the sūra of al-'Uqud. Here it is used in its concomitant meaning, which is the absence of grief and anger at the conduct of the enemies of the religion. The object of pardon is omitted because it is evident, meaning: pardon those who denied you and harmed you.

Al-jamil means good, and the intended meaning is complete pardon.

Furthermore, this verse contains a kind of radd al-'ajz 'ala al-sadr (a rhetorical device in which the end of a passage echoes its beginning). The placement of the waw at the beginning of this sentence is remarkable. This sentence is suitable to serve as a concluding generalization (tadhyil) to the accounts of the punished nations, showing that what befell them was deserved. It is part of God's justice in recompensing deeds according to what suits them. It is also suitable to serve as an introduction to the sentence that follows it, namely ﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming﴾. The intended meaning is the Hour of the recompense of those who denied Muhammad (ﷺ), that is, the Hour of Resurrection. On the first reading the waw is parenthetical (i'tiradiyya) or circumstantial (haliyya). On the second reading it is conjunctive ( 'atifa), joining one sentence to another and one predicate to another.

Page 75 (continued)

However, the conjunction may occur in both cases so that the sentence stands independently in conveying its content, because of its importance, even though it also completes what precedes it. What gave this sentence this remarkable position is the inimitable arrangement of the sentences (nazm al-jumal al-mu'jiz) and the movement from one purpose to another through the relevance that links them.

"The heavens and the earth and what is between them" includes all kinds of created beings, animals and inanimate things. It includes the nations that are on the earth and what befell them. It includes the angels charged with sending down punishment. It includes the cosmic events that struck the nations, such as earthquakes, thunderbolts and falling fragments.

The bi' in ﴿except with truth﴾ is of association (lil-mulabasa) and is connected to ﴿We created﴾. The meaning is: a creation associated with truth and accompanied by it, such that truth is manifest in all the conditions of created beings.

The association here is customary ('urfiyya). The manifestation of truth may be delayed relative to the creation of some conditions and events, with varying delay. Thus the association between creation and truth varies according to the states of the manifestation and concealment of truth. Yet truth does not remain hidden for long; it appears in the final outcome of affairs, as indicated by the saying of God, the Exalted: ﴿Rather, We hurl the truth against falsehood, and it crushes it, and behold, it vanishes﴾ (al-Anbiya', 21:18).

Truth here is the ordering of the conditions of created beings according to a system suited to wisdom and fitness, in good and evil, perfection and deficiency, elevation and abasement, in every kind, according to what befits its quiddity and reality and what sets it right and what it is fit for, in accordance with what the general order requires and not according to desires and appetites. When that described truth is evident, its existence accompanying the existence of what it is due to, the matter is clear. When the deviation of something from a fitting order appears, then through reflection and inquiry it becomes clear that behind that lies a fitness that required the suspension of the due accompaniment. Then truth is not changed in the end.

This interpretation is shown by the placement of the verse after the mention of the punishment of the nations that rebelled and oppressed. That punishment is a fitting recompense for their rebellion and corruption. Even though they were granted respite for a time, by a mercy from God and for the wisdom of preserving the habitation of part of the world for a period, they did not escape the punishment they deserved. That too is part of truth. Their respite was only truth, and the descent of punishment upon them was only truth when its causes arrived, namely their rebellion against their prophets. The same applies to the recompense of the Hereafter: it may be suspended in this world because of the suspension of what the general or particular wisdom required.

The purpose of this is to console the Prophet (ﷺ) for the harm he suffered from the polytheists, their denial, and their persistence in it until a known term.

In God's giving respite to the polytheists and then saving them from the punishment of extermination, there is a wisdom by which God's purpose is realized: the continuation of this religion and its spread in the world through the Arabs conveying it and carrying it to the nations.

﴿And We have certainly given you seven of the oft-repeated [verses] and the magnificent Qur'an﴾ is a parenthetical clause (i'tirad) placed between the sentence ﴿So pardon with gracious forgiveness﴾ [al-Hijr: 85] and the sentence ﴿Do not extend your eyes﴾ [al-Hijr: 88], and what follows it.

He follows the consolation and the promise with a reminder of favour, so that God reminds His Prophet ﷺ of the great blessing, and he is reassured that just as God has been good to him with the blessings already bestowed, He will fulfil the true promises He has made.

Thus the clause is coordinated (ʿatf) with the preceding clauses: it is the coordination of one theme with another theme, and of one narrative with another narrative. This marks the beginning of a new theme, namely the exaltation of the Qur'an and the belittling of the worldly life enjoyed by the polytheists.

The giving (ītāʾ) of the Qur'an means its bestowal, namely its being sent down to him and the revelation of it to him.

The verb (ātaynāka) ("We have given you") was chosen rather than (awḥaynā) ("We revealed") or (anzalnā) ("We sent down"), because giving is more evident in honour and favour.

Taking (al-Qur'ān) as coordinated with ﴿seven of the oft-repeated [verses]﴾ suggests that the seven oft-repeated [verses] are part of the Qur'an. This is what the majority of the exegetes (mufassirūn) have followed, and what the hadith mentioned below indicates.

The Qur'an is described as "oft-repeated" (al-mathānī) in Surat al-Zumar in His words ﴿God has sent down the best of discourse, a Book consistent, [and] repeating﴾ [al-Zumar: 23]. It is therefore established that the seven are things which are named with feminine grammatical agreement, because the feminine numeral noun (ism ʿadad al-muʾannath) is applied to them. It is also established that what is meant is verses or chapters of the Qur'an, and that (min) ("of") is partitive (tabʿīḍiyya), as is the usual function of (min) when it follows a numeral. And what is meant is parts of the Qur'an, verses or chapters, which have a distinction that required them to be singled out for mention from among the rest of the Qur'an. Also, al-mathānī are names of the Qur'an, as the verse of al-Zumar indicates and as the partitive (min) requires. The mathānī are entirely different from the seven, both in totality and in partiality, to make the coordination (ʿatf) valid.

The word (al-mathānī) may be the plural of (muthannā), with a dammah on the mim and a shaddah on the nūn, an passive participle derived from (thanna), meaning to repeat something once. It has been said that al-mathānī is the plural of (mathnāh), with a fatḥah on the mim, a sukūn on the thāʾ (the thāʾ being unvoweled and the letter being the thāʾ with three dots), and a feminine ending (tāʾ marbūṭa) at the end. In this case it is derived from the name of the number two (ism al-ithnayn).

The more correct view is that the seven oft-repeated [verses] are the Chapter of the Opening (Fātiḥat al-Kitāb), because it is repeated (yuthannā bihā), that is, it is repeated in every rakʿa of the prayer. So its derivation from the name of the number two is meant in the general sense of repetition, and this use is then a metonymy (majāz mursal) with the relation of generality (ʿalāqat al-iṭlāq), or a metonymic allusion (kināya), because repetition is a necessary concomitant. The dual form is used in this sense in His words ﴿Then return the gaze twice (kartayn)﴾ [al-Mulk: 4], meaning repeatedly (karrāt), and in the expressions of the Arabs: labbayka, saʿdayka, and dawālayka (all meaning "at your service, repeatedly").

Alternatively, (al-mathānī) is the plural of (mathnāh) used as a mīmī verbal noun (maṣdar mīmī) on the pattern (mafʿala), and the verbal noun is used to mean the passive object (al-mafʿūl).

Furthermore, if what is meant by the seven is seven verses, then the thing given is the Chapter of the Opening, because it consists of seven verses. This is what has been established from the Messenger of God ﷺ in the hadith of Abū Saʿīd ibn al-Muʿallā, Ubayy ibn Kaʿb and Abū Hurayra in the Ṣaḥīḥ, that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Umm al-Qurʾān is the seven oft-repeated [verses]." Therefore it is the most appropriate to rely upon.

This has already been mentioned in the discussion of the names of the Chapter of the Opening. The sense of repetition in the Chapter of the Opening is that it is repeated in the prayer.

From Ibn ʿAbbās: the seven oft-repeated [verses] are the seven long chapters (al-suwar al-sabʿ al-ṭiwāl), the first of which is al-Baqara and the last of which is Barāʾa (al-Tawba). It has also been said: they are the chapters that come after the chapters of the hundreds (dhawāt al-miʾīn).

The coordination of the Qur'an with the seven is the coordination of the whole with a part, for the purpose of generalisation, so that it is known that the giving of the whole Qur'an is a great blessing.

In the hadith of Abū Saʿīd ibn al-Muʿallā he said: The Prophet ﷺ said: "And the great Qur'an which he was given," on the interpretation that the word al-Qur'ān is in the nominative case as the subject (mubtadaʾ), and (alladhī ūtītuhu) ("which I was given") is its predicate (khabar).

The attribute "great" (al-ʿaẓīm) is applied to the Qur'an as an expression of exaltation of it.

If, however, what is meant by the seven is chapters, as is related from the saying of Ibn ʿAbbās and many of the Companions and the early generation (salaf), and they differed about identifying them in a manner that does not satisfy the heart, then their being unspecified is intended, so that people will attend to all the chapters of the Qur'an that were revealed, just as the Night of Power (laylat al-qadr) was left unspecified.

This is an explanatory resumptive clause (isti'naf bayani) answering what the preceding statement, ﴿وما خَلَقْنا السَّماواتِ والأرْضَ وما بَيْنَهُما إلّا بِالحَقِّ﴾ [al-Hijr: 85], brings to mind, and the question that arises in the soul about God's granting respite to those who deny, who are immersed in blessings and luxury, even though they have been threatened with wrath and punishment. So the clause ﴿لا تَمُدَّنَّ عَيْنَيْكَ﴾ serves as an explanation of what stirs in the listener's soul on this matter. Because it has this status, it is detached from the clause before it, in the manner of an explanation separated from what it explains.

Had the clause that came before it not served as a preparation for it and a general statement of its content, this clause would have been conjoined to it by a conjunction, because it would then be a mere prohibition with no connection to what precedes it. This is like its counterpart in God's words in Surat Ta-Ha: ﴿فاصْبِرْ عَلى ما يَقُولُونَ وسَبِّحْ بِحَمْدِ رَبِّكَ قَبْلَ طُلُوعِ الشَّمْسِ وقَبْلَ غُرُوبِها ومِن آناءِ اللَّيْلِ فَسَبِّحْ وأطْرافَ النَّهارِ لَعَلَّكَ تَرْضى﴾ [Ta-Ha: 130], followed by ﴿ولا تَمُدَّنَّ عَيْنَيْكَ إلى ما مَتَّعْنا بِهِ أزْواجًا مِنهم زَهْرَةَ الحَياةِ الدُّنْيا﴾ [Ta-Ha: 131]. Since the clause is detached here, it is understood that the preceding clause was intended as a preparation for this one. Had this clause been conjoined, this subtle meaning would not have been grasped from the arrangement of the discourse.

The word al-madd (extension) originally means increase, and it is applied to the stretching and lengthening of the body; one says: he extended his hand toward such-and-such, or he extended his leg on the ground. Then it was used figuratively for an increase in something, as in madad al-jaysh (reinforcements of the army), madd al-bahr (the tide of the sea), and al-madd fi al-'umr (lengthening of life). These usages are widespread and have become literal. Here, madd is used metaphorically for directing one's gaze and aspiring with it, likening this to extending the hand toward what one wishes to grasp. This is because what is forbidden is the gaze of admiration at the good state they enjoy in the ease of their lives despite their disbelief. That is, what you have been given is greater than that; had they been in a place deserving of care, they would have followed what We have given you, but they were content with the transient enjoyment, so they are not among those whose state should be admired.

The word al-azwaj (pairs/spouses) here may be taken in its well-known meaning, namely the disbelievers and their wives. The reason for singling them out is that their condition is the most complete form of enjoyment, since it combines all pleasures and comforts. It may also be taken as a metonymy (majaz) for categories (asnaf), a usage affirmed by al-Raghib. The reason for mentioning it in the verse is that the enjoyment to which the eye extends is not held by all disbelievers, but is the lot of their chiefs. That is, among them are those in a state of destitution, so consider them and see how disbelief and hardship of life have been combined for them.

The prohibition against grief includes every state of theirs that is capable of saddening and distressing the Messenger (peace be upon him). Among these is their disbelief, as God says: ﴿فَلَعَلَّكَ باخِعٌ نَفْسَكَ عَلى آثارِهِمْ إنْ لَمْ يُؤْمِنُوا بِهَذا الحَدِيثِ أسَفًا﴾ [al-Kahf: 6]. Among them is also the descent of punishment upon them like what befell them on the day of Badr, for they were the leaders of the people of Makkah. So the Messenger (ﷺ) might have grieved over their persistence until the punishment befell them. In this prohibition there is a kinaya (allusive expression) for the scant concern for them, and for the threat that what would grieve them would befall them; and a kinaya for the mercy of the Messenger (ﷺ) toward people.

Since this prohibition implies hardness of heart and severity, he therefore followed it, without doubt, with a command to gentleness toward the believers in His words ﴿واخْفِضْ جَناحَكَ لِلْمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ ("and lower your wing to the believers"). This is an interjected clause (i'tiracertainly, i'tiraD) intended as a safeguard, and it is like His words ﴿أشِدّاءُ عَلى الكُفّارِ رُحَماءُ بَيْنَهُمْ﴾ [al-Fath: 29] ("hard against the disbelievers, merciful among themselves").

Lowering the wing is a figurative representation (tamthil) of gentleness and humility, drawn from the condition of a bird when it wants to descend to alight: it lowers its wing, intending to approach. It does likewise when it plays with its female, for then it inclines to peacefulness and gentleness, or when it prepares to gather its young under its wings. Within this figurative scene there is a metaphor by implication (isti'ara makniyya), and the "wing" is an imaginative element (takhyil). We have expounded this in Surat al-Isra in His words ﴿واخْفِضْ لَهُما جَناحَ الذُّلِّ مِنَ الرَّحْمَةِ﴾ [al-Isra: 24] ("and lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy"). This figurative scene has become so widespread that it has become like a proverb for humility and softness in dealing with others. Its opposite is raising the wing, a figure for harshness and severity.

From the poetry of the scholar al-Zamakhshari, addressing one who was humble but then showed arrogance, which he mentioned in Surat al-Shu'ara:

"You are renowned for lowering the wing, so do not, in lofty rank, become an ajdal (a falcon)."

In this verse there is a preparation for what follows it, namely His words ﴿فاصْدَعْ بِما تُؤْمَرُ وأعْرِضْ عَنِ المُشْرِكِينَ﴾ [al-Hijr: 94] ("so proclaim what you are commanded and turn away from the polytheists"). The clause ﴿وقُلْ إنِّي أنا النَّذِيرُ المُبِينُ﴾ ("And say: Indeed, I am the clear warner") is conjoined to the clause ﴿ولا تَحْزَنْ عَلَيْهِمْ﴾ ("and do not grieve over them"). Thus, those to whom this statement is addressed are the ones spoken of by the preceding pronouns in His words "from them" (منهم) and "over them" (عليهم). The sense is: and say to them. This statement is meant as a severing of ties, that is, my duty is only to warn you. The indicator is the mention of warning rather than direct action, because warning suits those who deny, since warning is the notification of an event containing harm.

The word al-nadhir (warner) is on the pattern fa'il in the sense of muf'il, like al-hakim meaning al-muhkim (the one who makes firm), and darb wajI' meaning painful blow, i.e., one that causes pain.

The restriction derived from the pronoun of separation (damir al-fasl) and from the definiteness of the two components is a restriction by reversal (qasr qalb). That is: just as you suppose that you enrage me by your unbelief, I am indeed a clear warner, not bargaining with you for the attainment of your faith.

[p. 84]

Al-mubin: the one who clarifies and makes explicit.

[p. 82]

This is an explanatory resumptive clause (isti'naf bayani) answering what the preceding statement, ﴿وما خَلَقْنا السَّماواتِ والأرْضَ وما بَيْنَهُما إلّا بِالحَقِّ﴾ [al-Hijr: 85], brings to mind, and the question that arises in the soul about God's granting respite to those who deny, who are immersed in blessings and luxury, even though they have been threatened with wrath and punishment. So the clause ﴿لا تَمُدَّنَّ عَيْنَيْكَ﴾ serves as an explanation of what stirs in the listener's soul on this matter. Because it has this status, it is detached from the clause before it, in the manner of an explanation separated from what it explains.

Had the clause that came before it not served as a preparation for it and a general statement of its content, this clause would have been conjoined to it by a conjunction, because it would then be a mere prohibition with no connection to what precedes it. This is like its counterpart in God's words in Surat Ta-Ha: ﴿فاصْبِرْ عَلى ما يَقُولُونَ وسَبِّحْ بِحَمْدِ رَبِّكَ قَبْلَ طُلُوعِ الشَّمْسِ وقَبْلَ غُرُوبِها ومِن آناءِ اللَّيْلِ فَسَبِّحْ وأطْرافَ النَّهارِ لَعَلَّكَ تَرْضى﴾ [Ta-Ha: 130], followed by ﴿ولا تَمُدَّنَّ عَيْنَيْكَ إلى ما مَتَّعْنا بِهِ أزْواجًا مِنهم زَهْرَةَ الحَياةِ الدُّنْيا﴾ [Ta-Ha: 131]. Since the clause is detached here, it is understood that the preceding clause was intended as a preparation for this one. Had this clause been conjoined, this subtle meaning would not have been grasped from the arrangement of the discourse.

The word al-madd (extension) originally means increase, and it is applied to the stretching and lengthening of the body; one says: he extended his hand toward such-and-such, or he extended his leg on the ground. Then it was used figuratively for an increase in something, as in madad al-jaysh (reinforcements of the army), madd al-bahr (the tide of the sea), and al-madd fi al-'umr (lengthening of life). These usages are widespread and have become literal. Here, madd is used metaphorically for directing one's gaze and aspiring with it, likening this to extending the hand toward what one wishes to grasp. This is because what is forbidden is the gaze of admiration at the good state they enjoy in the ease of their lives despite their disbelief. That is, what you have been given is greater than that; had they been in a place deserving of care, they would have followed what We have given you, but they were content with the transient enjoyment, so they are not among those whose state should be admired.

The word al-azwaj (pairs/spouses) here may be taken in its well-known meaning, namely the disbelievers and their wives. The reason for singling them out is that their condition is the most complete form of enjoyment, since it combines all pleasures and comforts. It may also be taken as a metonymy (majaz) for categories (asnaf), a usage affirmed by al-Raghib. The reason for mentioning it in the verse is that the enjoyment to which the eye extends is not held by all disbelievers, but is the lot of their chiefs. That is, among them are those in a state of destitution, so consider them and see how disbelief and hardship of life have been combined for them.

The prohibition against grief includes every state of theirs that is capable of saddening and distressing the Messenger (peace be upon him). Among these is their disbelief, as God says: ﴿فَلَعَلَّكَ باخِعٌ نَفْسَكَ عَلى آثارِهِمْ إنْ لَمْ يُؤْمِنُوا بِهَذا الحَدِيثِ أسَفًا﴾ [al-Kahf: 6]. Among them is also the descent of punishment upon them like what befell them on the day of Badr, for they were the leaders of the people of Makkah. So the Messenger (ﷺ) might have grieved over their persistence until the punishment befell them. In this prohibition there is a kinaya (allusive expression) for the scant concern for them, and for the threat that what would grieve them would befall them; and a kinaya for the mercy of the Messenger (ﷺ) toward people.

Since this prohibition implies hardness of heart and severity, he therefore followed it, without doubt, with a command to gentleness toward the believers in His words ﴿واخْفِضْ جَناحَكَ لِلْمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ ("and lower your wing to the believers"). This is an interjected clause (i'tiracertainly, i'tiraD) intended as a safeguard, and it is like His words ﴿أشِدّاءُ عَلى الكُفّارِ رُحَماءُ بَيْنَهُمْ﴾ [al-Fath: 29] ("hard against the disbelievers, merciful among themselves").

Lowering the wing is a figurative representation (tamthil) of gentleness and humility, drawn from the condition of a bird when it wants to descend to alight: it lowers its wing, intending to approach. It does likewise when it plays with its female, for then it inclines to peacefulness and gentleness, or when it prepares to gather its young under its wings. Within this figurative scene there is a metaphor by implication (isti'ara makniyya), and the "wing" is an imaginative element (takhyil). We have expounded this in Surat al-Isra in His words ﴿واخْفِضْ لَهُما جَناحَ الذُّلِّ مِنَ الرَّحْمَةِ﴾ [al-Isra: 24] ("and lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy"). This figurative scene has become so widespread that it has become like a proverb for humility and softness in dealing with others. Its opposite is raising the wing, a figure for harshness and severity.

From the poetry of the scholar al-Zamakhshari, addressing one who was humble but then showed arrogance, which he mentioned in Surat al-Shu'ara:

"You are renowned for lowering the wing, so do not, in lofty rank, become an ajdal (a falcon)."

In this verse there is a preparation for what follows it, namely His words ﴿فاصْدَعْ بِما تُؤْمَرُ وأعْرِضْ عَنِ المُشْرِكِينَ﴾ [al-Hijr: 94] ("so proclaim what you are commanded and turn away from the polytheists"). The clause ﴿وقُلْ إنِّي أنا النَّذِيرُ المُبِينُ﴾ ("And say: Indeed, I am the clear warner") is conjoined to the clause ﴿ولا تَحْزَنْ عَلَيْهِمْ﴾ ("and do not grieve over them"). Thus, those to whom this statement is addressed are the ones spoken of by the preceding pronouns in His words "from them" (منهم) and "over them" (عليهم). The sense is: and say to them. This statement is meant as a severing of ties, that is, my duty is only to warn you. The indicator is the mention of warning rather than direct action, because warning suits those who deny, since warning is the notification of an event containing harm.

The word al-nadhir (warner) is on the pattern fa'il in the sense of muf'il, like al-hakim meaning al-muhkim (the one who makes firm), and darb wajI' meaning painful blow, i.e., one that causes pain.

That is: just as you suppose that you enrage me by your unbelief, I am indeed a clear warner, not bargaining with you for the attainment of your faith.

Page 85

﴿As We sent down upon the dividers﴾ ﴿who made the Qur'an into fragments﴾. The comparison conveyed by the particle *ka* (like) is a comparison to what was sent down upon the dividers.

*Mā* (what) is either a relative pronoun (*mawṣūlah*) or a verbal-noun particle (*maṣdariyyah*), and it is the element compared to (*al-mushabbah bihi*).

As for the element being compared (*al-mushabbah*), it may be the giving (*al-ītā'*) derived from the verb in ﴿We have given you seven of the oft-repeated [verses]﴾ [al-Ḥijr: 87]. That is, a giving like what We sent down, or like Our sending down upon the dividers. The giving of part of the Qur'an to the Prophet ﷺ is compared to what was sent down to him concerning the dividers, meaning: We sent it down upon the messengers of the dividers, according to the two interpretations of "the dividers" that follow.

It may also be that the element being compared is the warning (*al-indhār*) derived from His saying, ﴿Indeed, I am the clear warner﴾ [al-Ḥijr: 89], that is, the warning of punishment, from His saying, ﴿By your Lord, We will surely question them all﴾ [al-Ḥijr: 92] ﴿about what they used to do﴾ [al-Ḥijr: 93].

The style of speech on these two readings is a transition (*takhallus*) from consoling the Prophet ﷺ to threatening the polytheists who slandered the Qur'an, informing them that they will be held accountable for their slanders.

This is either an explicit threat, if "the dividers" is intended to refer to the same persons intended by the two pronouns in His saying, ﴿pairs of them, and do not grieve over them﴾ [al-Ḥijr: 88].

The particle *ʿalā* (upon) here carries the meaning of the causal *lām* (for), as in His saying, ﴿that you may glorify God for having guided you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185], and His saying, ﴿so eat of what they catch for you﴾ [al-Mā'idah: 4], and the verse of ʿAlqamah ibn Shayban from the Banu Taym Allah ibn Thaʿlabah:

Page 85 (continued)

*We fight the enemies on account of our sons, and on account of our insights, even if we do not see.*

The word *al-muqtasimīn* (the dividers) is an *iftiʿāl* form from *qassama*, meaning to make something into parts. The *iftiʿāl* pattern here implies effort in doing the action.

"The dividers" may refer to a group of polytheists from Quraysh, who were sixteen men; we shall mention their names. In that case, "the Qur'an" refers to the proper name given to this book, the scripture of Islam.

It may also refer to groups of the People of the Book who divided their scripture into parts, some of which they disclosed and some of which they forgot. In that case, "the Qur'an" is a verbal noun used in its linguistic meaning, namely, what is read from their books. Or they divided the scripture of Islam, accepting part of it, which agreed with their religion, and rejecting part of it, which opposed what they held.

The meaning of "the dividers" has been stated in a general way, and its specification is given by the relative clause describing them in His saying, ﴿who made the Qur'an into fragments﴾. Therefore it is not possible that "the dividers" refers to anyone other than the two groups mentioned just above.

The meaning of division and fragmentation here is the division of attributes and states, not the division of the essence itself.

"The Qur'an" here may refer to the name designated as the proper name of the scripture of Islam, or it may refer to the scripture that is read, in which case it includes the Torah and the Gospel.

*ʿIḍīn* is the plural of *ʿiḍah*, which means a part or piece of something. Its original form is *ʿuḍw*, from which the *wāw* that is the final radical was dropped and replaced with a *hāʾ*, like the *hāʾ* in *sanah* and *shafah*. The dropping of the radical was intended to lighten the word, since a *wāw* at the end of a word becomes heavy when pausing upon it, so they substituted a letter for it, so that the word would not remain at two letters. They made the substitute a *hāʾ*, because it is the letter best suited to the state of pausing. The plural of *ʿiḍah* in the sound masculine plural pattern is an irregular (*shādh*) form.

Page 86

On both interpretations given above of what is meant by "the Qur'an" in this verse, "the dividers who made the Qur'an into fragments" are the People of the Book, the Jews and the Christians. They denied part of what was sent down to them, and the name "the Qur'an" was applied to their scripture because it is a book that is read. They disclosed some of it and concealed some of it. God, exalted is He, said, ﴿You make it into scrolls, displaying some and concealing much﴾ [al-Anʿām: 91]. In what they concealed, they resembled the polytheists in what they rejected of the Qur'an sent down to Muhammad ﷺ. They also made the Qur'an sent down to Muhammad ﷺ into fragments, accepting part of it, which agreed with their own circumstances, and rejecting part of it, which opposed their desires, such as the abrogation of their law and the nullification of the sonship of Jesus to God, exalted is He. So when the polytheists asked them, "Is the Qur'an true?", they would say, "Part of it is true and part of it is false." Thus their disagreement resembled the disagreement of the polytheists in describing the Qur'an with differing attributes, such as their saying "fables of the ancients," "the speech of a soothsayer," and "the speech of a poet."

It is related from Qatadah that the dividers were a group of polytheists of Quraysh whom al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah gathered when the time of the Hajj came. He said, "The delegations of the Arabs will come to you, and they have heard of the matter of this companion of yours, so agree on one opinion concerning him." Sixteen men undertook this, and they divided the approaches and roads of Mecca in order to turn people away from Islam. Some of them would say, "Do not be deceived by this Qur'an, for it is magic." Some would say, "It is poetry." Some would say, "It is the speech of a madman." Some would say, "It is the word of a soothsayer." Some would say, "It is the fables of the ancients which he has written down." Thus they divided the Qur'an into kinds according to the differences in its attributes.

These men were: Ḥanẓalah ibn Abi Sufyan, ʿUtbah ibn Rabiʿah and his brother Shaybah, al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, Abu Jahl ibn Hisham and his brother al-ʿĀs, Abu Qays ibn al-Walid, Qays ibn al-Fakih, Zuhayr ibn Umayyah, Hilal ibn ʿAbd al-Aswad, al-Sa'ib ibn Sayfi, al-Nadr ibn al-Ḥarith, Abu al-Bakhtari ibn Hisham, Zamaʿah ibn al-Ḥajjaj, Umayyah ibn Khalaf, and Aws ibn al-Mughirah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 15, verses 92–93:

﴿So by your Lord, We will surely call them to account, all of them﴾ ﴿for what they used to do.﴾ The fa' (al-fa', the particle of consequence) here is li-l-tafri' (indicating a consequence), and this is a consequence drawn from what preceded it in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And indeed, the Hour is coming, so overlook with gracious forgiveness﴾ [al-Hijr: 85].

The waw is for the oath (li-l-qasam), so what is derived (al-mufarra') is the oath and its response (jawab), and the purpose of the oath is to emphasize the report. The Messenger (ﷺ) is not one who doubts the truthfulness of this threat, but the emphasis applies to what the report contains of a threat directed at the object of the accusative pronoun in (lanas'alannahum).

The description of the Lord (rabb) as attached to the pronoun of the Prophet (ﷺ) is an indication that the questioning which is sworn to contains a share of honoring him, namely the questioning of God of those who denied, concerning their denial of him, the questioning of a Lord who is angered on behalf of His Messenger (peace be upon him).

The questioning (su'al) is used in one of its implied meanings, which is the punishment of the one questioned, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Then you will surely be questioned that Day about the bliss﴾ [al-Takathur: 8]. So it is a warning to both groups.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 15, verses 94–96:

﴿So proclaim openly what you are commanded, and turn away from the polytheists.﴾ ﴿Indeed, We have sufficed you against the mockers,﴾ ﴿those who set up another god alongside Allah. They will come to know.﴾ This is a consequence (*tafri'*) of the statement ﴿And We have certainly given you seven of the oft-repeated [verses]﴾ [al-Hijr: 87], both explicitly and by implication, as a consolation for what he faces from the denial of his people.

These verses were revealed in the fourth or fifth year of the Prophethood, while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was hiding in the house of al-Arqam ibn Abi al-Arqam.

It is related from 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) remained in hiding until ﴿So proclaim openly what you are commanded﴾ was revealed, and then he and his companions went out." What is meant is that when the surah of al-Muddaththir was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was calling people in secret. Whoever among the people embraced Islam, when he wished to pray, would go to some of the mountain ravines to pray in hiding from the polytheists. The polytheists came upon them, mocking them and disparaging their prayer. A clash then occurred between them and Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, in which Sa'd wounded a man from among the polytheists. After that incident, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his companions entered the house of al-Arqam near al-Safa. They performed the prayer there and continued in this way for three years or more. Then the words of His Exalted saying ﴿So proclaim openly what you are commanded﴾ were revealed, and with their revelation the Messenger (ﷺ) gave up hiding in the house of al-Arqam, and openly proclaimed the call to Islam.

*Al-sad'* means openly declaring and publicizing. Its original sense is splitting, as in the cracking of a vessel (*infisad al-ina'*), meaning its breaking. From this, the word *al-sad'* is used for the necessary implication of splitting, which is the appearance of a matter that was hidden behind the thing that has been split. Thus, what is meant here is open declaration and proclamation.

The referent of (*ma tu'mar*, "what you are commanded") is the call to Islam.

The purpose of including in the command everything the Messenger (ﷺ) was commanded to convey is the reason the complement of (*tu'mar*) is omitted. Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 15, verses 97–99:

﴿And We certainly know that your breast is distressed by what they say.﴾ ﴿So glorify your Lord with His praise and be among those who prostrate.﴾ ﴿And worship your Lord until there comes to you the certainty.﴾

Since the warning implied that they would be given respite for a little while, as He said, ﴿And give them respite a little﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 11], and as the particle of future (ḥarf al-tanfīs) in His words ﴿But they will come to know﴾ [al-Ḥijr: 96] indicates, God reassured His Prophet (ﷺ) that He was aware of his distress over their harm and their slander, and of their words of polytheism and mockery. So He commanded him to be steadfast and to entrust the matter to his Lord, because the wisdom in their being given respite is [known to Him]. For this reason the sentence opens with the oath particle (lām al-qasam) and the particle of affirmation (ḥarf al-taḥqīq).

The addressee is not one whose belief in God's report could be troubled by doubt. Rather, the affirmation is a metonymy (kināyah) for attentiveness to the reported matter and for its being a matter of special concern from God. So the sentence is conjoined to the sentence ﴿Indeed, We suffice you against the mockers﴾ [al-Ḥijr: 95], or it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl).

"Constriction of the breast" (ḍīq al-ṣadr) is a figurative expression (majāz) for the troubling of the soul, and it has already been discussed in His words ﴿and your breast is constricted by it﴾ [Hūd: 12] in the surah of Hud.

The command to glorify God and to declare Him free of what they ascribe to Him of partners is derived (fa-urrī'a) from the sentence ﴿We certainly know﴾. That is: you should declare your Lord free [of partners], so their polytheism will not harm you. Moreover, glorification (tasbīḥ) may be used in its metonymic meaning alongside its literal meaning, so it conveys a rejection of the polytheists in what they say. That is: in repelling them, confine yourself to rejecting their speech. This is like His words ﴿Say: Glory be to my Lord! Was I but a human messenger?﴾ [al-Isrā': 93].

The preposition bā' in ﴿bi-ḥamdi rabbika﴾ [with the praise of your Lord] denotes accompaniment (muṣāḥabah). The sense is: "glorify your Lord with His praise." The second object was omitted from the first, being indicated by the second. Glorifying God is declaring Him free [of imperfection] by saying, "Glory be to God" (subḥāna Allāh).

The commands in ﴿and be among those who prostrate﴾ and ﴿and worship your Lord﴾ are used to demand continuity.

The expression ﴿min al-sājidīn﴾ [among those who prostrate] is more emphatic in describing the attribute of prostration than "prostrating" (sājidan), as has been discussed in His words ﴿and be with the truthful﴾ [al-Tawbah: 119] in the surah of Bara'ah, and His words ﴿He said: I seek refuge in God from being among the ignorant﴾ [al-Baqarah: 67] in the surah of al-Baqarah, and their like.

The "prostrators" (al-sājidūn) are those who pray. So the meaning is: "Persist in prayer, you and those who are with you."

This is not a place of a prostration of recitation (sajdat al-tilāwah) according to any of the jurists of the Muslims. In the tafsir of al-Qurṭubī, it is reported from Abū Bakr al-Naqqāsh that Abū Ḥudhayfah, perhaps meaning Abū Ḥudhayfah al-Yamān ibn al-Mughīrah al-Baṣrī, one of the companions of 'Ikrimah, and he was weak in ḥadīth, and al-Yamān ibn Ri'āb, regarded it as an obligatory prostration of recitation.

Ibn al-'Arabī said: I witnessed the imam at the niche (miḥrāb) of Zakariyyā in Bayt al-Maqdis prostrate at this point when reciting it during the tarāwīḥ of Ramadan, and I prostrated with him in it. The prostration of the imam is strange, and the prostration of Abū Bakr ibn al-'Arabī with him is stranger, given the consensus (ijmā') that there is no prostration here. So prostrating in it is considered an addition, and it is undoubtedly an innovation (bid'ah).

Certainty (al-yaqīn) is that which is definite, with no doubt in it, and it is the victory that God promised him.

[Page 93]

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surat al-Naḥl

This surah was called by the early generations (al-salaf) "Surat al-Naḥl," and this is its well-known name in the copies of the Qur'an, in books of tafsir, and in books of Sunnah.

The reason for naming it thus is that the word "al-naḥl" (the bee) is not mentioned in any other surah.

It is reported from Qatadah that it is also called "Surat al-Ni'am" (the surah of blessings), that is, with a kasrah on the nūn and a fatḥah on the 'ayn. Ibn 'Aṭiyyah said: because God enumerated in it the blessings upon His servants.

It is Meccan according to the majority, and this is reported from Ibn 'Abbās and Ibn al-Zubayr. It was said that except for three verses, which were revealed in Medina when the Prophet (ﷺ) returned from the Battle of Uhud, namely His words ﴿And if you punish, then punish with the like of what you were punished with﴾ [al-Naḥl: 126] to the end of the surah. It was said: they were revealed concerning the abrogation (naskh) of the Prophet's (ﷺ) intention to mutilate seventy of the polytheists, should God grant him victory over them, as retaliation for their mutilation of Ḥamzah.

It is reported from Qatadah and Jābir ibn Zayd that its beginning is Meccan up to His words ﴿And those who emigrated for God after they had been wronged﴾ [al-Naḥl: 41], and from there to the end of the surah is Medinan.

What will come in the tafsir of His words ﴿Have they not seen the birds subjected in the air of the sky?﴾ [al-Naḥl: 79] indicates that some of the surah is Meccan and some is Medinan, and some of it was revealed after the emigration to Abyssinia, as His words indicate ﴿Then indeed your Lord, for those who emigrated after they had been tried﴾ [al-Naḥl: 110] show; and some of it was revealed later than the surah of al-An'ām, because of His words in this surah ﴿And for those who were Jews We prohibited what We have related to you before﴾ [al-Naḥl: 118], meaning by what He related before His words ﴿And for those who were Jews We prohibited every animal with claws﴾ [al-An'ām: 146] and the verses thereafter.

Al-Qurṭubī mentioned that it is reported from 'Uthmān ibn Maẓ'ūn: when this verse was revealed, I recited it to Abū Ṭālib, and he was amazed and said: "O family of Ghālib, follow my nephew and you will prosper, for by God, God sent him to command you with noble character."

Aḥmad narrated from Ibn 'Abbās that when this verse was revealed, 'Uthmān ibn Maẓ'ūn was sitting with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) before he embraced Islam. He said: "That was when faith settled in my heart, and I loved Muḥammad (ﷺ)."

It is also narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded by God to place it in this position in this surah.

This surah was revealed after the surah of al-Anbiyā', and before the surah of "Alif Lām Mīm" al-Sajdah. It is counted as the seventy-second in the chronological order of the revelation of the surahs.

Its number of verses is one hundred and twenty-eight, without any disagreement. It is reported from al-Khafājī, on the authority of al-Dānī, that it has nearly ninety-something verses, and this is probably an error, a distortion, or an omission.

The purposes of this surah: most of what the surah contains is a repeated presentation of diverse evidences for God's exclusive divinity (infirād Allāh bi-al-ulūhiyyah), evidences for the corruption of the religion of polytheism and the exposure of its abomination, and evidences for the affirmation of the prophethood of Muḥammad (ﷺ) and the sending down of the Qur'an upon him (ﷺ).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 15, verses 97–99:

﴿And We certainly know that your breast is distressed by what they say.﴾ ﴿So glorify your Lord with His praise and be among those who prostrate.﴾ ﴿And worship your Lord until there comes to you the certainty.﴾

Since the warning implied that they would be given respite for a little while, as He said, ﴿And give them respite a little﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 11], and as the particle of future (ḥarf al-tanfīs) in His words ﴿But they will come to know﴾ [al-Ḥijr: 96] indicates, God reassured His Prophet (ﷺ) that He was aware of his distress over their harm and their slander, and of their words of polytheism and mockery. So He commanded him to be steadfast and to entrust the matter to his Lord, because the wisdom in their being given respite is [known to Him]. For this reason the sentence opens with the oath particle (lām al-qasam) and the particle of affirmation (ḥarf al-taḥqīq).

The addressee is not one whose belief in God's report could be troubled by doubt. Rather, the affirmation is a metonymy (kināyah) for attentiveness to the reported matter and for its being a matter of special concern from God. So the sentence is conjoined to the sentence ﴿Indeed, We suffice you against the mockers﴾ [al-Ḥijr: 95], or it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl).

"Constriction of the breast" (ḍīq al-ṣadr) is a figurative expression (majāz) for the troubling of the soul, and it has already been discussed in His words ﴿and your breast is constricted by it﴾ [Hūd: 12] in the surah of Hud.

The command to glorify God and to declare Him free of what they ascribe to Him of partners is derived (fa-urrī'a) from the sentence ﴿We certainly know﴾. That is: you should declare your Lord free [of partners], so their polytheism will not harm you. Moreover, glorification (tasbīḥ) may be used in its metonymic meaning alongside its literal meaning, so it conveys a rejection of the polytheists in what they say. That is: in repelling them, confine yourself to rejecting their speech. This is like His words ﴿Say: Glory be to my Lord! Was I but a human messenger?﴾ [al-Isrā': 93].

The preposition bā' in ﴿bi-ḥamdi rabbika﴾ [with the praise of your Lord] denotes accompaniment (muṣāḥabah). The sense is: "glorify your Lord with His praise." The second object was omitted from the first, being indicated by the second. Glorifying God is declaring Him free [of imperfection] by saying, "Glory be to God" (subḥāna Allāh).

The commands in ﴿and be among those who prostrate﴾ and ﴿and worship your Lord﴾ are used to demand continuity.

The expression ﴿min al-sājidīn﴾ [among those who prostrate] is more emphatic in describing the attribute of prostration than "prostrating" (sājidan), as has been discussed in His words ﴿and be with the truthful﴾ [al-Tawbah: 119] in the surah of Bara'ah, and His words ﴿He said: I seek refuge in God from being among the ignorant﴾ [al-Baqarah: 67] in the surah of al-Baqarah, and their like.

The "prostrators" (al-sājidūn) are those who pray. So the meaning is: "Persist in prayer, you and those who are with you."

This is not a place of a prostration of recitation (sajdat al-tilāwah) according to any of the jurists of the Muslims. In the tafsir of al-Qurṭubī, it is reported from Abū Bakr al-Naqqāsh that Abū Ḥudhayfah, perhaps meaning Abū Ḥudhayfah al-Yamān ibn al-Mughīrah al-Baṣrī, one of the companions of 'Ikrimah, and he was weak in ḥadīth, and al-Yamān ibn Ri'āb, regarded it as an obligatory prostration of recitation.

The prostration of the imam is strange, and the prostration of Abū Bakr ibn al-'Arabī with him is stranger, given the consensus (ijmā') that there is no prostration here. So prostrating in it is considered an addition, and it is undoubtedly an innovation (bid'ah).

Certainty (al-yaqīn) is that which is definite, with no doubt in it, and it is the victory that God promised him.
